items.title: The Rate Path Wildcard (October 2026 Housing Market Forecast)
items.description: The Rate Path Wildcard (October 2026 Housing Market Forecast) Written by Mischa Fisher on October 23, 2026 The decline in existing home sales is forecasted to accelerate in the fourth quarter, as our moving average of newly pending existing home sales dropped 12.8% in Zillow's latest weekly data. Total annual sales are still forecasted to finish up slightly in 2026 relative to 2025, given the lower share of sales volume the fourth quarter contributes. Inventory growth is expected to increase 6.6% Y/Y in Q4, alongside home value growth of only 0.7% Rent growth is continuing to build, with rents expected to grow 2.4% in multifamily and 3.2% in single-family in the fourth quarter. Given the volatility in mortgage rate paths, mathematical models are more likely to require revision. As we’ve continued to note in a variety of commentary : the current economic cycle is a strange one. We’ve added a rate hiking cycle with its expected contractionary effects on top of a weak housing market rather than on top of a strong market, defying the normal story we expected from Ed Leamer’s characterization that housing is the business cycle. As a result we’re expecting October existing home sales (we’ll release full month statistics on November 5th ) to be down considerably year-over-year. (On a rolling average weekly basis, newly pending listings dropped a whopping 12.8% year-over-year in our latest weekly data ). But the most important question right now for both housing and the economy is what else is slowed by high interest rates, and how soon. If the past is prologue we expect at some point a return to more normal market dynamics, where housing leads the business cycle. This necessarily means something else in the economy would need to slow first, the question is when. For example, we’ve seen recent selloffs in the AI related equity market paired with some nervousness about expectations for return on invested capital. So if this or another part of the economy outside of housing does indeed slow, then we’d expect investors to migrate to the safety of longer dated securities, mortgage rates to come down, home sales to rise, and housing to lead the business cycle again. But while there are early signs of this, it hasn’t happened yet. So while our current outlook is based on the current rate path, I think it’s increasingly likely that the actual path we follow will either be notably better or worse than what the math would predict. (Worse, if inflation isn’t brought under control, or better if inflation and/or growth expectations drop sooner rather than later). With that caveat on the current math noted, here’s what our latest forecast predicts. items.title: Zillow: CPI Shelter Forecast, October 2026
items.description: Zillow: CPI Shelter Forecast, October 2026 Zillow forecasts 2.8% rent inflation, 3.3% OER inflation annually in October, as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Written by Treh Manhertz on October 27, 2026 New shelter inflation numbers from the Bureau of Labor Statistics are scheduled to be released on Friday, November 10, 2026 at 8:30 ET. Key Takeaway CPI housing inflation is expected to stay elevated through the end of the year and into 2027. We currently forecast annual rent inflation to finish 2026 up around 3.1% and OER up near 3.4%. September’s reading on Owners’ Equivalent rates showed growth at the upper end of expectations, but this is unlikely to be the start of a great rise. Shelter disinflation has effectively plateaued in the near-term. New-lease rents have been growing at their fastest pace of 2025-2026, putting a damper on the declines in measured housing inflation. Forecasts for on-market rents have been revised higher for the past few months. Current trends suggest that by year-end, the annual rate of growth will be roughly equal between new-lease rents and CPI rents, keeping a floor under inflation. items.title: New Home Sales Declined in September as Builders Focused on Inventory Management
items.description: New Home Sales Declined in September as Builders Focused on Inventory Management Written by Kenny Lee on October 27, 2026 What happened New home sales fell slightly by 0.6% to 676 thousand SAAR in September, essentially holding firm at 680 thousand in August but 5.3% below a year ago. The median price of new homes sold declined 3.9% from a year ago, to $400,400. As homebuilders delay new construction, the number of new homes on the market fell 2.3% year over year to 476 thousand homes in September — marking the 11th consecutive month of annual decline. Inventory adjustment has been a counterbalance to cooler inventory. At the latest sales pace, it would take about 8.4 months to clear the inventory, up slightly from 8.2 months a year ago. Smaller and more affordable units constituted a larger share of total sales, with 70% of homes selling below $500,000 in September. As elevated mortgage rates keep buyers on the sidelines, the share will likely continue to rise. By comparison, 66% of new homes sold were below this price point in September last year. Inventory management would remain the number one priority for builders For builders, the ongoing shift toward smaller homes was prudent and necessary. While mortgage rates soared above 7% in September, homebuilders have been navigating elevated rates, in addition to their wild swings, for a while. Builders will remain focused on inventory management, especially as competition from the resale market increases. Zillow’s September report shows resale inventory rose 2.5% year over year, marking the 34th consecutive month of annual gains. In addition, 27.4% of sellers reduced asking prices as they adapt to shifting buyer demand. Building smaller homes is a win-win for both buyers and builders. For buyers, a lower entry point helps them navigate the challenging affordability landscape. For builders, they can keep their inventory moving even as buyers see more options in the resale market. items.title: Pending Home Sales Decreased 7.3% in September
items.description: Pending Home Sales Decreased 7.3% in September Section Menu NAR Media Contacts Statistical Release Schedule Op-Eds & Letters to the Editor NAR Fact Sheet NAR in the News More October 20, 2026 Media Contact: Media Relations Residential Real Estate , Promoting Home Ownership , Financing & Credit , Mortgages & Home Financing Share View and share this infographic Month-Over-Month 7.3% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions Year-Over-Year 11.3% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions View Pending Home Sales Report WASHINGTON (October 20, 2026) – Pending home sales in September decreased by 7.3% month-over-month and 11.3% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS ® Pending Home Sales report . The report helps the real estate ecosystem—including agents, homebuyers and sellers—better understand the housing market by providing data on the level of home sales under contract. Month-over-month pending home sales declined in all four major U.S. regions. The West had the largest decrease, followed by the South, Midwest and Northeast. Year-over-year pending home sales also declined in all four regions. “Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates,” said NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun. “Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates.” “Given that mortgage rates have already risen much more than the Federal Reserve’s short-term interest rate hikes, mortgage rates could be topping out,” Yun said. “However, increasing energy prices and the resulting inflationary pressure are highly uncertain.” “Despite the difficulty of obtaining a mortgage, the limited number of distressed properties is ensuring steady home prices,” Yun added. “Buyers and sellers may simply be holding back until mortgage rates move favorably.” September 2026 National Pending Home Sales 7.3% decrease month-over-month 11.3% decrease year-over-year September 2026 Regional Pending Home Sales Northeast 4.2% decrease month-over-month 9.4% decrease year-over-year Midwest 6.5% decrease month-over-month 8.7% decrease year-over-year South 8.2% decrease month-over-month 12.0% decrease year-over-year West 9.2% decrease month-over-month 15.0% decrease year-over-year At the local level, pending home sales fell year-over-year even in the strongest markets. Among the 50 largest metro areas, the following 10 markets posted the smallest annual declines in pending home sales, according to data from Realtor.com ® Economics: Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin, TN (-2.0%) Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (-2.1%) San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont, CA (-3.5%) San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, CA (-4.6%) Buffalo-Cheektowaga, NY (-5.6%) Richmond, VA (-5.8%) Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, TX (-5.9%) Pittsburgh, PA (-6.2%) Memphis, TN-MS-AR (-6.3%) San Antonio-New Braunfels, TX (-7.1%) About the National Association of REALTORS ® The National Association of REALTORS ® is involved in all aspects of residential and commercial real estate. The term REALTOR ® is a registered collective membership mark that identifies a real estate professional who is a member of the National Association of REALTORS ® and subscribes to its strict Code of Ethics . For free consumer guides about navigating the homebuying and selling transaction processes—from written buyer agreements to negotiating compensation—visit facts.realtor . # # # *The Pending Home Sales Index is a leading indicator for the housing sector, based on pending sales of existing homes. A sale is listed as pending when the contract has been signed but the transaction has not closed, though the sale usually is finalized within one or two months of signing. Pending contracts are good early indicators of upcoming sales closings. However, the amount of time between pending contracts and completed sales is not identical for all home sales. Variations in the length of the process from pending contract to closed sale can be caused by issues such as buyer difficulties with obtaining mortgage financing, home inspection problems, or appraisal issues. The index is based on a sample that covers about 40% of multiple listing service data each month. In developing the model for the index, it was demonstrated that the level of monthly sales-contract activity parallels the level of closed existing-home sales in the following two months. An index of 100 is equal to the average level of contract activity during 2001, which was the first year to be examined. By coincidence, the volume of existing-home sales in 2001 fell within the range of 5.0 to 5.5 million, which is considered normal for the current U.S. population. items.title: FOMC Leaves Rate Unchanged
items.description: Economic Coverage FOMC Leaves Rate Unchanged By Danielle Hale Oct 28, 2026 The Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee (FOMC), the rate-setting body that meets roughly eight times per year, left the Federal Funds rate unchanged at its October meeting in a target range of 3.75 to 4.0 percent. This hold follows a 25 basis point hike in September, and was supported by 10 of the 12 voting members. Two voters, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, dissented, because they preferred to raise the rate by a quarter percentage point instead of holding. Even though the Fed left its policy rate unchanged in October, the market is anticipating another 2 to 3 hikes over the next 6 to 8 months which would mean a high-end rate range of 4.5 to 4.75 percent. This is slightly above the high-end of Fed funds rate projections made in September, and would position the Fed funds rate roughly halfway between its December 2025 to September 2026 low of 3.5 to 3.75 percent and its 5.25 to 5.5 percent prior peak. While the market and the Fed both seem to agree that some monetary policy restriction is warranted, most investors currently expect more restriction than the Fed has projected. Why further rate hikes are expected Since the September FOMC meeting, when the Fed pushed its rate 25 basis points higher, companies slowed hiring and summer job gains were revised down by 60,000 jobs . The unemployment rate remains relatively stable at 4.2 percent and layoffs are low, but the labor market is less dynamic than is ideal. Meanwhile, inflation surprised to the upside, with the CPI rising 0.6% in September, bringing the annual headline inflation rate to 3.7% as the cost of gas and energy rose sharply. Energy was not the only driver, however, and core CPI, which strips out the cost of food and energy, rose 2.6% in September. Taken together, these indicators suggest that the Fed is likely to continue its focus on inflation, which will likely warrant additional rate hikes. What this means for housing, and homebuyers and sellers Investors have made a round-trip in risk pricing since just before the September Fed meeting. The 10-year yield rose from just under 5 percent to more than 5.3 percent before dipping just under 5 percent in recent days, while mortgage rates climbed from just below 7 percent to more than 7.4 percent. Mortgage rates have not dropped back to their mid-September level, and the housing market is feeling the effects. Pending home sales in September dropped to their lowest level on record according to the National Association of Realtors as buyers and sellers have largely disengaged with the housing market for now. In August and September, existing-home sales dropped below a 4 million sales pace, and are likely to remain low through the rest of the year. Home shoppers shopping in this environment can still set themselves up for a better mortgage rate by boosting their credit, making a higher down payment, and, most importantly, shopping around for a mortgage. Those hoping to make a home purchase in the months ahead should plan for further mortgage rate volatility and rate-proof their home shopping budget by testing out a range of possible mortgage rates so they’ll be prepared to react.

items.title: HOUSTON HOMEBUYING ACTIVITY EASES IN SEPTEMBER AS MORTGAGE RATES RISE
items.description: HOUSTON HOMEBUYING ACTIVITY EASES IN SEPTEMBER AS MORTGAGE RATES RISE Home prices remain steady as buyers navigate elevated mortgage rates HOUSTON -- (October 14, 2026) -- As Houston's housing market moved into the fall season, homebuying activity eased compared to a year ago as buyers faced mortgage rates greater than 7%. Despite higher borrowing costs, home prices remained steady. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' September 2026 Housing Market Update, 7,030 single-family homes were sold, down 5.7% from a year earlier. The average home price edged up by 0.7% to $421,311. The median price, which represents the midpoint of all homes sold, was essentially unchanged at $325,000. Buyers had more choices than they did a year ago. There were 40,192 homes for sale across the Greater Houston area in September, up 6.3% from a year earlier. "Higher mortgage rates are making buyers look more closely at what they can comfortably afford," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC - Houston. "People are taking a little more time, weighing their options and focusing on long-term affordability. Stable prices and a broad selection of homes are helping keep opportunities within reach." Conventional 30-year residential mortgage rates averaged 6.86% in September according to Freddie Mac, up from 6.35% a year ago. Assuming a 20% down payment, buyers of median-priced homes in the Houston area saw monthly principal and interest payments rise from $1,622.29 a year ago to $1,705.41 in September. That's up $83.12 monthly or $997.40 annually. On a weekly basis, Freddie Mac reported average mortgage rates for September rising from 6.71% initially to 6.76%, then 6.95% and rising to 7.03% the final week of the month. Rates in the first two weeks of October continued to climb to 7.28% and then 7.40%, respectively. Housing Market Overview Across all property types, 8,181 properties were sold in September, down 6.4% from a year ago. Total dollar volume reached $3.45 billion, which is down 2.1% from the same time last year. Active listings across all property types rose 5.0% to 62,002 available properties. Single-Family Homes Update In September, single-family home sales totaled 7,030, down 5.7% compared to a year ago. The average sales price rose from $418,256 to $421,311. The median price edged down from $325,990 to $325,000. Inventory expanded from 5.1 months to 5.5 months. Nationwide, there was a 4.8 months supply, according to the National Association of Realtors. Homes took an average of 58 days to sell, compared with 56 days a year ago. Pending listings, which represent homes under contract but not yet closed, declined 11.6% to 6,789. This suggests some buyers are taking more time before committing to a purchase. Broken out by housing segments, single-family home sales performed as follows: $1 - $99,999: increased 3.7% (111 transactions) $100,000 - $149,999: increased 5.6% (188 transactions) $150,000 - $249,999: decreased 8.4% (1,359 transactions) $250,000 - $499,999: decreased 5.7% (3,878 transactions) $500,000 - $999,999: increased 0.6% (1,189 transactions) $1M and above: decreased 8.2% (304 transactions) HAR also reports on existing single-family home sales, which held steady compared to last September with 5,062 closings. The average price declined 1.1% to $427,110, while the median price was unchanged at $325,000. HAR will publish its September 2026 Rental Market Update on Wednesday, October 21. For HAR's Monthly Activity Snapshot (MAS) of the September 2026 trends, please CLICK HERE to access a downloadable PDF file. Townhome/Condominium Update The townhome and condominium market faced stronger headwinds in September. Sales declined 21.0% from a year ago, with 323 properties sold. The average sales price decreased 4.6% to $261,052. The median price fell 9.1% to $209,000. Active listings rose 6.9% to 3,609 available properties. Inventory rose from 8.0 months to 9.3 months. Pending sales declined 15.9%, from 440 to 370. Houston Real Estate Highlights in September • Single-family home sales decreased 5.7% year over year. • Pending sales declined 11.6% to 6,789. • Active listings increased 6.3% to 40,192 homes. • Days on Market for single-family homes increased from 56 to 58 days. • The single-family average price increased 0.7% to $421,311. • The single-family median price remained essentially unchanged at $325,000. • Inventory expanded from 5.1 months to 5.5 months. • Total property sales declined 6.4% with 8,181 transactions. • Total dollar volume decreased 2.1% to $3.45 billion. items.title: Los Angeles Rental Report 2026Q3: Renters Catch a Break as New Supply Pushes Rents Lower; Buying Still Costs Nearly $5,000 More a Month
items.description: Los Angeles Rental Report 2026Q3: Renters Catch a Break as New Supply Pushes Rents Lower; Buying Still Costs Nearly $5,000 More a Month By Jiayi Xu , Danielle Hale Oct 29, 2026 Highlights In 2026Q3, the median asking rent in Los Angeles County registered at $2,554,—down $96, or 3.6%, from a year earlier. The median asking rent for 0-2 bedrooms in L.A. County was $2,239, reflecting a decline of $88 (-3.8%) from the previous year. Meanwhile, rent for 3+ bedroom units dropped by $70 (-1.9%) compared to 2025Q3, standing at $3,571. For renters in L.A. County : Buying costs far more than renting. In 2026Q3, a median-priced home cost $4,716 more a month than renting one, nearly 185% higher, even though the monthly buying cost fell about 2% as home prices dropped. Mortgage rates above 7% could erase that relief. At 7%, the same home would cost about $7,456 a month, roughly where it stood a year ago, erasing the savings from lower prices In the third quarter of 2026, the median asking rent for all rental properties listed on Realtor.com in Los Angeles County was $2,554, a decline of $96, or 3.6%, compared with a year ago. While the county experienced a temporary dip in rents during the pandemic, asking rents quickly rebounded to pre-pandemic levels and peaked in the summer of 2022. Since then, a surge in new multifamily construction has put sustained downward pressure on rent. In the most recent quarter, the median asking rent in Los Angeles County was $340, or 11.7%, below its 2022 peak. In addition, Los Angeles County renters are overwhelmingly local. In the third quarter of 2026, more than half (61.3%) of online traffic to L.A. County rental listings originated from within the county, with an additional 15.5% coming from elsewhere in California. Out-of-state renters accounted for 19.8% of traffic, while international traffic represented 3.4%. Breaking down by bedroom type, the median asking rent for 0-2 bedroom units in Los Angeles County was $2,239 in 2026Q3, a decline of $88 or 3.8%, from a year ago. Larger units with three or more bedrooms saw a comparatively modest softening, with a median asking rent of $3,571 — down $70, or 1.9%, year-over-year. The steeper rent decline among smaller units suggests renters in that segment are experiencing greater pricing relief. The surge in ADUs across Los Angeles County may partially explain this trend. As those permitted units complete construction — typically requiring 6 to 18 months from permit to occupancy — a growing wave of new small rental units has been entering the market, adding downward price pressure concentrated in the smaller unit segment. County Rents by Unit Size, 2026Q3 Unit Size Median Asking Rent Rent YoY vs. Peak Overall $2,554 -3.6% -11.7% 0-2 beds $2,239 -3.8% -14.7% 3+ beds $3,571 -1.9% -11.3% City of Los Angeles: Relief from the peak, but still out of reach for many In the third quarter of 2026, the median asking rent for rental properties listed on Realtor.com in the City of Los Angeles was $2,708, reflecting a decline of $92, or 3.3%, from a year earlier. Consistent with the broader L.A. County trend, rents in the City of Los Angeles have been on a downward trajectory since peaking in the summer of 2022. While the current median remains $158, or 5.5%, above pre-pandemic levels, renters today are saving $363 per month, or 11.8%, compared to the 2022 peak, translating to $4,356 in annual savings. Nevertheless, in order to afford a typical home in the city of Los Angeles, a minimum annual income of $108,320 is required— 22.1% higher than the city's estimated median household income of $88,730 1 High mortgage rates squeeze renters hoping to buy Renters may be catching a break, but for most renters who want to become homeowners in L.A. County, homeownership remains out of reach. On top of that, with mortgage rates now above 7%, higher borrowing costs could push homeownership even further out of reach for renters who want to buy. In 2026Q3, buying a typical home in L.A. County costs $4,716 more per month than renting one. Buying got slightly cheaper over the past year because home prices fell, even as mortgage rates rose. The median listing price dropped 3.2% to $970,000 over the past year, which more than offset a small increase in the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate, from 6.57% to 6.68%. As a result, the estimated monthly cost of buying a median-priced home fell about 2.1%, or $159, from a year earlier, to $7,270. But that relief may not last. Rates surpassed 7% in late-September and remain well- above this mark. At 7%, the same home price would cost about $7,456 a month, roughly where it stood a year ago, erasing the monthly payment savings from lower prices. Methodology To determine the monthly cost of buying a home, we find the median listing price for homes in Los Angeles County. As first-time homebuyers plan lower down payments, we assume a 10% down payment and use the 30-year fixed mortgage rate during the quarter to calculate a monthly mortgage payment. We also include the HOA fees, taxes, and homeowners insurance as part of the costs. L.A. rental data as of 2026Q3 for all units advertised for rent on Realtor.com®. Rental units include apartments as well as private rentals (condos, townhomes, single-family homes). We use rental sources that reliably report data each month within L.A. county. To calculate the median asking rent for each quarter, we first obtain the median asking rent for each month within that quarter and then take the average of the three months. Month-Over-Month 1.5% increase in existing-home sales to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.99 million in September 1.9% increase in unsold inventory to 1.60 million units, equal to 4.8 months’ supply Year-Over-Year 2.2% decrease in existing-home sales 1.3% increase in median existing-home sales price to $417,500 WASHINGTON (October 13, 2026) – Existing-home sales increased by 1.5% month-over-month and decreased by 2.2% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS ® Existing-Home Sales report. The report provides the real estate ecosystem, including agents, homebuyers and sellers, with data on home sales, prices and inventory. Month-over-month sales increased in the South and West, held steady in the Midwest and declined in the Northeast. Year-over-year sales declined in all four regions. “Despite the small monthly gain on a seasonally adjusted basis, August and September marked the two slowest months for home sales this year,” said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun. “Further increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home.” “Higher inventory and lengthening days on market give buyers improved negotiating power. Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers,” Yun said. National Snapshot Total Existing-Home Sales for September Existing-home sales increased 1.5% month-over-month. Existing-home sales decreased 2.2% year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.99 million. Inventory in September Total housing inventory reached 1.60 million units, up 1.9% from August and 4.6% from September 2025. Unsold inventory represented a 4.8-month supply, unchanged from August and up from 4.5 months one year ago. Median Sales Price in September The median existing-home price for all housing types was $417,500. Prices increased 1.3% from one year ago ($412,300), marking the 39th consecutive month of year-over-year price gains. Housing Affordability in September The Housing Affordability Index registered 105.4, down from 106.7 one year ago. Affordability declined year-over-year in three of the four regions: Northeast: -4.5% Midwest: -3.1% South: -0.4% West: +1.0% Single-Family and Condo/Co-op Sales Single-Family Homes in September Sales increased 2.0% month-over-month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.64 million, down 1.9% from September 2025. The median single-family home price was $422,700, up 1.2% year-over-year. Condominiums and Co-ops in September Sales decreased 2.8% month-over-month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 350,000. Sales were down 5.4% from September 2025. The median condo/co-op price was $363,700, up 1.2% year-over-year. Regional Snapshot for Existing-Home Sales in September Northeast Sales declined 2.1% month-over-month to an annual rate of 470,000. Sales were down 4.1% from September 2025. Median price: $523,600, up 4.7% year-over-year. Midwest Sales were unchanged month-over-month at an annual rate of 930,000. Sales were down 2.1% year-over-year. Median price: $329,600, up 3.1% year-over-year. South Sales increased 2.8% month-over-month to an annual rate of 1.86 million. Sales were down 0.5% from September 2025. Median price: $361,000, up 0.2% year-over-year. West Sales increased 2.8% month-over-month to an annual rate of 730,000. Sales were down 5.2% year-over-year. Median price: $613,600, down 0.3% from September 2025. REALTORS® Confidence Index for September Median time on market: 33 days, up from 31 days in August and unchanged from September 2025. First-time buyers represented 31% of sales, up from 30% in August and 30% one year ago. Cash sales accounted for 27% of transactions, unchanged from last month and down from 30% one year ago. Individual investors and second-home buyers accounted for 20% of transactions, up from 15% last month and one year ago. Distressed sales represented 2% of transactions, unchanged from both last month and one year ago. Mortgage Rates The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.86% in September, up from 6.67% in August and 6.35% one year ago, according to Freddie Mac. About the National Association of REALTORS ® The National Association of REALTORS ® is involved in all aspects of residential and commercial real estate. The term REALTOR ® is a registered collective membership mark that identifies a real estate professional who is a member of the National Association of REALTORS ® and subscribes to its strict Code of Ethics . For free consumer guides about navigating the homebuying and selling transaction processes, from written buyer agreements to negotiating compensation, visit facts.realtor . Information about NAR is available at nar.realtor . This and other news releases are posted in the newsroom at nar.realtor/newsroom . Statistical data in this release, as well as other tables and surveys, are posted in the Research and Statistics section. items.title: Homeownership Rate Holds at 65.5% in Q3
items.description: Economic Coverage , Homeownership Homeownership Rate Holds at 65.5% in Q3 By Hannah Jones Oct 28, 2026 2026 Q3 Homeownership and Housing Vacancy Key Takeaways Homeownership rate holds steady. The U.S. homeownership rate was 65.5% in Q3 2026, statistically unchanged from both the prior quarter (65.0%) and a year earlier (65.3%). The rate continues to plateau in a narrow low-to-mid-65% band, with affordability pressures and limited supply showing little sign of easing their grip on the market. Homeowner vacancy remains low and steady. The homeowner vacancy rate held at 1.2% in Q3, virtually unchanged from both the prior quarter and a year earlier. Rental vacancy reaches its highest level in over a decade. The rental vacancy rate rose to 7.6%, up both quarter-over-quarter (7.3%) and year-over-year (7.1%), its highest level since 2014. Renting remains a critical pressure valve, though conditions vary by geography. With a national rental vacancy rate of 7.6%, rental markets continue to offer more flexibility for households unable to buy. Principal cities (8.8%) remain looser than suburbs (6.5%) and non-metro areas (6.4%), which were statistically similar to each other. The South leads in vacancy levels, while the Northeast and West saw the clearest year-over-year shifts. The South posted the highest rental vacancy rate (9.2%) and homeowner vacancy rate (1.5%) of any region, though neither was statistically different from a year ago. Rental vacancy rose significantly in the Northeast (5.0% to 6.2%) and the West (6.0% to 6.7%). Ownership slipped among 35-to-44-year-olds, while older households gained. Homeownership among 35-to-44-year-olds fell from 61.1% to 60.1% year-over-year. Households under 35 remain the lowest at 36.6%, statistically unchanged from 37.5% a year earlier. Meanwhile, 65+ homeownership rose from 77.9% to 79.1%. Racial ownership gaps remain entrenched. Homeownership among Black households fell from 45.7% to 44.4% year-over-year, while White homeownership rose from 74.0% to 75.1%. All other groups did not see statistically significant shifts. What happened this quarter The U.S. homeownership rate held at 65.5% in the third quarter of 2026, statistically unchanged compared with both the prior quarter (65.0%) and a year earlier (65.3%). While the rate remains within the narrow low-to-mid-65% range that has characterized the market in recent years, it continues to run well below the 2020 pandemic-era peak. Mortgage rates pushed back above 7% in late September for the first time in more than a year, which could weigh on would-be buyers heading into the fourth quarter. The homeowner vacancy rate held at 1.2% in Q3 2026, virtually the same as the previous quarter and the previous year. While homeowner vacancy remains below pre-pandemic norms, the recent pick up in inventory could mean vacancy drifts higher if demand is not sufficient to absorb supply. The rental vacancy rate rose to 7.6% in the third quarter, higher than both the previous quarter (7.3%) and the previous year (7.1%). With mortgage rates moving back above 7%, renting continues to stand out as a more affordable alternative to homeownership. However, climbing rental vacancy suggests that units are sitting empty as affordability pressure may discourage household formation. Vacancy was highest in principal cities (8.8%). Suburbs (6.5%) and non-metro areas (6.4%) were lower and not statistically different from each other. Regional differences remain pronounced . The South recorded the highest rental vacancy rate at 9.2%, followed by the Midwest (7.1%), the West (6.7%), and the Northeast (6.2%). The Midwest was higher than the Northeast and statistically similar to the West, while the Northeast and West were not statistically different from each other. Of the four regions, only the Northeast (up from 5.0%) and West (up from 6.0%) saw a statistically significant year-over-year increase in rental vacancy. Rental vacancy has stalled in the South as the wave of supply has subsided . The post-pandemic construction boom flooded these markets with new supply, but as multifamily construction has slowed, vacancy growth has stalled. On the ownership side, the South again led with the highest homeowner vacancy rate at 1.5%, while the other three regions saw vacancy between 0.9% and 1.1%. The Midwest continues to stand out for its high homeownership rate, reaching 69.5% in Q3 2026, though not statistically different from a year earlier, and remains well above the South (67.2%), Northeast (62.9%), and West (60.6%). Different outcomes by race/ethnicity Homeownership rates by race and ethnicity were mixed year over year. In the third quarter, the rate for non-Hispanic White householders rose to 75.1% from 74.0%, while the rate for Asian, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander householders was statistically unchanged at 62.3%. The rate for Black householders fell to 44.4% from 45.7%, and the rate for Hispanic householders was statistically unchanged at 48.1%. The gap between the highest and lowest rates remains more than 30 percentage points, underscoring the persistence of structural barriers to ownership. Different outcomes by age Ownership among younger households remains low, while older householders saw improvement. Homeownership among those under 35 was the lowest of any age group at 36.6%, statistically unchanged from 37.5% a year earlier. Homeownership among households aged 35 to 44 fell from 61.1% in Q3 of 2025 to 60.1% in Q3 of 2026. Ownership in the 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 cohorts held steady at 70.4% and 75.4%, respectively, while the 65+ group saw a 1.2 percentage point improvement to 79.1%. Ample starter-home inventory is crucial for young homeownership, and availability varies significantly across the country .

items.title: October 2026 Commercial Real Estate Market Insights Report
items.description: Commercial Real Estate Market Insights October 2026 Commercial Real Estate Market Insights Report Share Download the report pdf (3.5 MB) Economic conditions were mixed in August. The economy continued to grow, but at a slower pace. The labor market remained relatively steady, while inflation was still elevated. At the same time, interest rates remained high, suggesting that borrowing costs are likely to stay elevated in the near term. With little change in the broader economy, commercial real estate also continued a similar path in August. Some sectors improved further, while others remained mostly steady. Below is a summary of the performance of each major commercial real estate sector in August of 2026: The office market continued to stabilize in August as positive annual absorption strengthened and vacancy edged lower. Improving demand and firmer rent growth suggest the sector is moving further from the prolonged period of occupancy losses, though the recovery remains uneven. Class A continued to lead leasing activity, while Class B remained pressured by tenant move-outs despite substantial inventory removal. Class C also recorded negative absorption, although its comparatively low vacancy continues to distinguish it from the rest of the market. Multifamily conditions improved further in August as solid demand combined with a continued slowdown in new supply, allowing absorption to remain above deliveries. This rebalancing is helping the sector work through excess inventory, with vacancy declining and rent growth gradually strengthening, though pricing power remains limited. Class A continued to benefit from demand exceeding new supply, while Class B maintained resilient absorption and modestly improving fundamentals. Class C also improved, returning to slightly positive absorption while retaining the lowest vacancy among the three classes. Fundamentals across the retail sector remained resilient in August as positive absorption broadened across major formats and vacancy stayed near historically low levels. General retail remained the largest source of demand, while Neighborhood Centers, Malls, and Power Centers all posted positive absorption. Supply growth continues to outpace demand, creating some risk of modest vacancy pressure as new space is delivered. Even so, limited availability continues to support rents, with Neighborhood and Power Centers posting the strongest growth among the major formats. Conditions across the industrial sector continued to normalize in August as stronger absorption narrowed the gap with new supply and helped limit further vacancy pressure. Demand more than doubled from a year earlier, signaling continued progress in working through excess inventory, though rent growth remained restrained. Logistics accounted for most leasing activity, while specialized facilities maintained the tightest vacancy. Flex continued to lag the broader market, with negative absorption and the highest vacancy among the three major property types. Hospitality performance remained relatively steady in August, although occupancy continued to trail pre-pandemic levels as remote work and softer corporate travel constrained business-focused markets. ADR and RevPAR stayed well above 2019 benchmarks, helping support operating results despite weaker occupancy. Investment activity remained restrained as high borrowing costs and economic uncertainty continued to weigh on investor appetite. Back to top

items.title: HOUSTON RENTAL DEMAND REMAINS STRONG IN SEPTEMBER
items.description: HOUSTON RENTAL DEMAND REMAINS STRONG IN SEPTEMBER Leasing activity increases as rental choices expand HOUSTON -- (October 21, 2026) -- The Greater Houston rental market continued to see strong demand in September as elevated mortgage rates kept affordability top of mind for many consumers. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' September 2026 Rental Market Update , 3,761 single-family homes were leased compared to 3,645 in September 2025. Lease prices remained relatively stable. The average lease price edged down 0.6% to $2,333, while the median price declined 1.4% to $2,150. "Renters are staying active across the Houston area, and there are more homes for them to choose from," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC - Houston. "With mortgage rates rising, renting remains an attractive option for some would-be homebuyers who are still weighing whether to make a purchase. Renting provides flexibility while they consider their options." The townhome and condominium rental market recorded an especially strong September. Leased listings jumped 26.3% year over year, rising from 525 properties to 663. The average lease price increased 3.5% to $1,958, while the median price rose 5.9% to $1,800. New listings increased 4.8% to 1,192 properties, and active listings rose 8.8% to 2,456. Townhomes and condominiums took an average of 48 days to lease, four days longer than in September 2025. items.title: HUFFMAN AREA LEADS HOUSTON'S HOTTEST COMMUNITIES WITH TRIPLE-DIGIT GROWTH
items.description: Media Contacts Brittany Aucion Director of Communications (713) 629-1900 ext.1256 Send email Isabela Ortiz Consumer Marketing Specialist (713) 629-1900 ext.1254 Send email HUFFMAN AREA LEADS HOUSTON’S HOTTEST COMMUNITIES WITH TRIPLE-DIGIT GROWTH Needville Area and Sugar Land East follow with significant gains in third quarter HOUSTON -- (October 26, 2026) -- From newly built homes to more affordable price points, buyers are finding opportunities in communities across the Greater Houston area that are seeing some of the region's biggest gains in home sales. According to HAR's latest Hottest Communities in the Houston Area report, the Huffman Area led all communities with a 166.7% year-over-year increase in home sales during the third quarter of 2026. Home sales climbed from 63 to 168 properties sold, putting the community back in the top spot after ranking second in the previous quarter. Needville Area followed with an 80.6% increase in transactions, while Sugar Land East posted a 52.9% gain. Waller (up 45.7%) and Humble Area East (up 36.7%) rounded out the top five. New construction continues to account for a significant share of sales in several of the hottest communities. Newly built homes represented 87.6% of transactions in Waller, 81.5% in Needville Area and 62.5% in the Huffman Area. Home prices varied across the top 10 communities, with seven reporting average prices below the Houston-area average of $421,311. The Huffman Area recorded an average home price of $276,515, while Needville Area averaged $335,494. "Buyers are looking for value, and these communities are showing that there are still opportunities to find it," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC - Houston. "New construction is helping meet that demand by offering more choices at different price points. It's encouraging to see that kind of activity across so many parts of the Houston area." The report also highlights the top-performing luxury communities in Greater Houston, where average home prices are at least $1 million. The Tanglewood Area led the luxury rankings for the third consecutive quarter, with an 84.6% year-over-year increase in home sales. Transactions rose from 13 to 24, with an average home price of $2,705,229. items.title: Why home prices and new home sales aren’t as hot as today’s reports show
items.description: Home prices were actually improving on a year-over-year basis recently, which should make you question anyone who has been saying this. Also, even though new home sales data beat estimates while mortgage rates were elevated, you should view it through the lens of a rate-buydown marketplace. The new home sales sector has been living off rate buydowns from builders, whereas the existing home sales market hasn’t. So, let's look at both reports and try to explain what is happening. Home prices From Case Shiller : The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index posted a 2.1% annual gain for August 2026, up from a 1.9% rise in the previous month. U.S. home values fell in real terms for the 15th consecutive month, as August’s 3.4% inflation ran roughly 1.3 percentage points above the 2.1% home price gain. A nearly 9-percentage-point gap separated August’s strongest market (Chicago +6.7% YoY) and its weakest (Seattle -2.0% YoY), underscoring the strong regional divergence in home price trends. My home-price forecast for this year is -0.62%, as I've said in the Housing Market Tracker articles for a while, and I think it will be hard to reach in 2026. Even though mortgage rates are elevated and demand is finally taking a noticeable hit as inventory rises, I don’t think I will have enough time in 2026 to be right. Home prices have been up 1%-2% year over year every month. The Case Shiller index lags our data by a few months. Inventory actually went negative in mid-June . As we have talked about throughout the year, the year-over-year comps were going to be hard to show growth until mid-June. Then the supply-to-demand equilibrium improved as rates fell, giving us a bit more pricing power. But mortgage rates started to go above 7% in September , and the dynamic shifted. So our data is a few months ahead of the Case-Shiller index, and price growth will get hit, but keep in mind year-over-year comps are easy to beat now. Because we hardly had any price growth last year, all in all, this is still a very healthy housing market in the sense that inventory is up, price growth is cooling down and wages are outpacing home prices. That wasn't the case in 2023, when mortgage rates rose to 8% but home prices were up 6%. Home-price growth should be cooling down when the Case Shiller catches up, but as you can see now, if you wasted one second of your life on national home price crash doomers from 2012-2026, you wasted your precious time on untalented hacks. New home sales From Census : New Home Sales Sales of new single-family houses in September 2026 were at a seasonally-adjusted annual rate of 676,000, according to estimates released jointly today by the U.S. Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development. This is 0.6 percent (±13.8 percent)* below the August 2026 rate of 680,000, and is 5.3 percent (±12.5 percent)* below the September 2025 rate of 714,000 . This is the same story I have talked about for years: the new home sales data — if you remove the COVID burst in sales and the decline from that peak — has really gone nowhere for 10 years. New home sales are still at 2019 levels, even though demand for housing is there with lower rates. In fact, if we applied the same rate profile to the existing home sales market, we would have seen growth years ago. However, I don’t believe existing home sales would be trending at 2019 levels if mortgage rates were between 4.75% and 5.75%, which is where rates are with builder buydowns. They would be higher for sure, but not at 2019 levels, as that would amount to 1 to 1.3 million more existing home sales than today’s levels. So for now, after revisions, new home sales don’t really break above 730,000 or go below 570,000 on a monthly basis; we can have a few prints above or below these levels, but we've been stuck in this sales channel for years now. One positive story going untold: builders are slowly reducing excess supply ; for housing starts to really grow, this pool needs to shrink, and new home sales need to grow. One reason housing starts aren’t even worse today is that buy-downs have kept demand at 2019 levels while builders work through excess supply. Much more work remains, but it hasn’t gotten worse even with higher rates; the question is whether this can continue into 2027 with rates above 7% and profit margins falling. Conclusion All in all, nothing too surprising with the Case-Shiller Home Price Index or new home sales data if you look at it with the same lens I do. I think some people might be surprised since rates are elevated right now and the existing home sales demand has been softening up, but again, the Case Shiller index lags, and the new home sales market is still working with the sub-6 % mortgage market world. So as long as you look at it in that context, today’s data makes a little bit more sense. Tomorrow the Federal Reserve meets and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will give his remarks. I gave a preview of this in today's episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast and tried to explain why the Fed won’t hike rates tomorrow. Related More: Home Price Index Home Sales

items.title: Las Vegas multifamily rent pressures persist despite leasing gains
items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Las Vegas multifamily market report here.HighlightsLas Vegas multifamily operating conditions remain soft, with elevated vacancy, rising concessions and declining rents. Net absorption has exceeded deliveries in 2026, but the improved supply-demand balance has yet to translate into rent growth.Stabilized vacancy reached 9.1% at the end of the third quarter, flat from the prior quarter but up 20 basis points from one year earlier. Vacancy remains 30 basis points below the year-end 2025 rate.Asking rents averaged $1,479 per month by the end of September, down 1.4% year over year and 0.9% lower than in the prior quarter, the second consecutive quarterly decline.Investment sales volume during the third quarter totaled roughly $209 million across five deals, with Class B properties accounting for four of the five deals. The year-to-date median sale price reached $225,900 per unit.Las Vegas multifamily market overviewLas Vegas multifamily fundamentals remain under pressure despite improved absorption and a slowdown in new deliveries in 2026. Net absorption has exceeded deliveries by roughly 650 units year to date, after trailing them by nearly 1,700 units in 2025. Absorption has already surpassed the full-year 2025 total, supported by continued job growth, while completions have slowed as fewer projects remain under construction. The recovery has been concentrated in the suburbs, where Summerlin/Spring Valley, Henderson and Enterprise/South Paradise captured more than two-thirds of that demand with less than half of the metro’s inventory. Rent growth has been slower to rebound. Asking rents remain below year-ago levels, with the steepest declines in older urban core submarkets, where vacancy is above 10%. By contrast, rents in suburban submarkets remain close to year-ago levels.Investment activity in 2026 has become concentrated in two of the suburban submarkets that are leading the leasing recovery. Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson accounted for roughly three-quarters of metro sales volume through the third quarter, up from 43% in 2025. Third-quarter activity followed the same pattern, with three of the five trades located in those two submarkets. Pricing has remained stable in Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson, with median sale prices near $250,000 per unit in both submarkets, above levels elsewhere in the metro, where recent trades have skewed toward smaller, older properties. The median price across the Las Vegas region has remained near its 2025 level, highlighting the influence of property location on pricing trends.Employment:Area employers added 21,400 jobs year over year. Image Area payrolls increased by 21,400 jobs year over year as of the third quarter of 2026, a gain of 1.8%. Hiring slowed from the first half of the year and held below the 10-year average annual growth rate of 2.4%.Professional and business services remained the leading source of new jobs, adding 10,900 positions and expanding 6.3% year over year. Education and health services added 5,400 jobs, while leisure and hospitality, the largest local employment sector, shed 2,200 positions, a 0.7% decline.Hyve Solutions, a manufacturer of storage and AI computing hardware, is establishing a new production facility in North Las Vegas. The project, the largest of four business expansions approved for state tax incentives in August, is expected to create 240 jobs over the next two years.Forecast: Employers are forecast to add roughly 20,000 jobs in 2026, a 1.7% increase, maintaining a pace similar to 2025. Development and permitting:Developers completed roughly 600 units in the third quarter. Image Developers completed roughly 600 units in the third quarter, all in Central Las Vegas. Year-to-date deliveries total around 2,600 units, down 23% from the same period in 2025. Roughly 6,100 units were under construction at the end of the third quarter, down more than 25% from the end of 2025, which is expected to ease supply pressure on operators heading into 2027. Six active projects in Spring Valley total more than 2,000 units.Multifamily permitting activity is regaining momentum. Developers pulled permits for 1,130 multifamily units in the third quarter, more than double the total from one year earlier.Forecast: Developers are expected to complete roughly 4,000 units in 2026, in line with both the 2025 total and the 10-year average.Vacancy:Vacancy ended the third quarter at 9.1% Image Stabilized vacancy ended the third quarter at 9.1%, up 20 basis points year over year. Despite the annual increase, net absorption has exceeded deliveries in 2026, pushing vacancy down 30 basis points from year-end 2025.Class B properties account for roughly 70% of net absorption this year, with vacancy flat year over year at 9.0%. Class A vacancy edged up to 8.4%, while Class C, the only tier with negative net absorption in 2026, posted the highest vacancy at 10.0%.Suburban submarkets continue to pull away from the urban core. Summerlin/Spring Valley, Henderson and Enterprise/South Paradise captured more than two-thirds of net absorption this year, each with vacancy below 7.5%. Las Vegas Strip vacancy rose 170 basis points year over year to 12.1%.Forecast: Vacancy is expected to tick up 20 basis points to 9.3% by year-end 2026, though it would remain 10 basis points below the year-end 2025 rate.Rents:Asking rents averaged $1,479 per month. Image Asking rents averaged $1,479 per month in the third quarter, down 0.9% from the prior quarter and 1.4% year over year. Rents have declined for two consecutive quarters, erasing the gain recorded at the start of the year.Rent performance varied across submarkets. Henderson posted a modest 1.0% year-over-year rise to $1,580 per month, while rents declined in each submarket with vacancy rates above 10%, including a 5.0% annual drop on the Las Vegas Strip.Class A was the only tier to post annual rent growth, up 0.7% to $1,772 per month. items.title: S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index Reports Annual Gain in August 2026 - Oct 27, 2026
items.description: Press Releases Media Contacts Social Media Directory Press Kit Press Releases S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index Reports Annual Gain in August 2026 The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index posted a 2.1% annual gain for August 2026, up from a 1.9% rise in the previous month. U.S. home values fell in real terms for the 15th consecutive month, as August's 3.4% inflation ran roughly 1.3 percentage points above the 2.1% home price gain. A nearly 9 percentage point gap separated August's strongest market (Chicago +6.7% YoY) and its weakest (Seattle -2.0% YoY), underscoring the strong regional divergence in home price trends. NEW YORK , Oct. 27, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- S&P Dow Jones Indices (S&P DJI) today released the August 2026 results for the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Indices. More than 27 years of history are available for the data series and can be accessed in full by going to www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/index-family/indicators/sp-Cotality-case-shiller . Cotality continues to have transaction delays from the recording office in Wayne County, the most populous county in the Detroit metro area. These delays impacted the August transaction data and, therefore, no valid August 2026 update of the Detroit S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index will be provided for the October 27, 2026, release date. There was, however, enough data to calculate a valid July 2026 update, which is provided in Tables 2 and 3. S&P DJI will continue to provide updates to the Detroit index values for the month(s) with missing sale transactions data. ANALYSIS "U.S. home prices declined in real terms for the 15th consecutive month in August 2026, though the gap narrowed as nominal home price growth strengthened," said Rebecca Kaufman, Associate Director of Commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices. "The S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller National Home Price Index rose 2.1% year-over-year in August, up from 1.9% in July, while consumer prices increased 3.4% (the same year over year gain as in July 2026). "Chicago led all metros for the sixth consecutive month, posting a 6.7% annual gain, followed by New York (6.2%) and Cleveland (4.3%). Download Q3 2026 Report Key RETAIL Takeaways For Q3 2026 Retail demand rebounded in Q3. Retail net absorption totaled 3.5 msf in Q3, the second-strongest quarterly reading since Q4 2023. Year-to-date absorption turned positive at 1.2 msf, while national vacancy held steady at 5.9%, well below the 7.4% historical average. Rent growth is moderating, but supply constraints remain supportive. Annual asking rent growth slowed to 2.2% year-over-year (YOY), with national asking rents reaching $25.82 per square foot (psf). Vacancy remains historically low, while new construction continues to be limited. Just 2.3 msf was delivered in Q3 and the development pipeline represents just 0.4% of existing inventory. This limited supply should help support stable fundamentals even if demand growth slows. Hot summer spending. Despite persistent inflation and low consumer sentiment, spending did not slow. Retail sales rose 6.0% YOY (4.3% YOY excluding gasoline stations). Unemployment remained near historic lows at 4.2%. However, household finances are showing signs of pressure, with the personal saving rate falling to a four-year low of 4.1% in August. Consumer spending is increasingly concentrated among the top 20% of earners, who now account for nearly 60% of personal outlays. For the data behind the commentary, download the full Q3 2026 U.S. Retail Report. Balanced Strength Across Regions National shopping center absorption reached 3.5 msf in Q3, bringing year-to-date (YTD) absorption into positive territory at 1.2 msf. Over the past four quarters, net absorption totaled 5.2 msf, reflecting a gradual recovery in retail space demand. The West continues to be a bright spot, absorbing 1.4 msf and remaining the only region with positive absorption in every quarter this year. Fourteen of its 22 markets posted positive absorption in Q3, led by Phoenix (+457,000 sf), Inland Empire (+345,000 sf) and Orange County (+275,000 sf). Regional asking rents rose 1.1% YOY. Construction remains concentrated in the South, which accounted for 52% of national completions YTD. The South was the only region to record an increase in vacancy during the quarter, reflecting new supply, particularly in strip centers. Even so, vacancy remained low at 5.7%, the tightest among the major regions. Knoxville and Nashville posted strong vacancy declines of 70 basis points (bps) quarter-over-quarter (QOQ). In the South, several secondary markets continue to outperform on rent growth. Charlotte, Baltimore, Raleigh/Durham and San Antonio each recorded annual asking rent growth above 4.0%, outpacing many larger metropolitan markets. The Northeast absorbed 1.2 msf in Q3, and eight of the 11 markets recorded vacancy declines, including New York City, Boston and Philadelphia, largely due to absorption in neighborhood and power centers. The Midwest led the major regions in asking rent growth at 3.6%. Columbus (7.2%), Cincinnati (7.1%) and St. Louis (5.6%) ranked in the top five for highest YOY rent growth. Other notable YOY rent growth markets are in the South, led by Palm Beach (9.8%) and Louisville (6.4%). Consumer Resilience Faces Persisting Headwinds Consumer fundamentals remained healthy in Q3. Unemployment held at 4.2%, labor force participation rose to 61.8%, and retail sales posted solid gains. However, underlying pressures remain. Inflation continues to outpace wage growth, and the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate by 25 bps. If sustained, higher borrowing costs, a cooling job market and pressure on real disposable income could weigh on spending. Geopolitical risk from the Middle East conflict remains a watchpoint. Higher energy prices have raised costs for gasoline, transportation, food and other goods. Nonetheless, households continue to spend despite higher prices. Our baseline assumes energy prices gradually moderate over the coming quarters, which should help ease pressure on household budgets. Consumer spending is increasingly bifurcated by income. Higher-income households continue to benefit from elevated equity market valuations, which support spending through the wealth effect. Lower- and middle-income households face a tougher environment as living costs erode purchasing power, favoring grocery, discount and value-oriented retailers over discretionary categories. items.title: US home price insights — October 2026
items.description: Overview: National single-family home price growth reaccelerated modestly in August, rising 1.8% year-over-year compared to 1.6% in July. Severe inventory shortages driven by sub-4% mortgage rate lock-ins and lack of new construction kept strong year-over-year gains in Illinois (6.8%), Connecticut (6.3%), with Indiana and New Jersey (5.6%). Condominiums and townhomes rose by only 0.1% year-over-year, reflecting persistent drag from rising HOA assessments and insurance costs. National home price growth August 2026 data Source: Cotality ‍ Affordability meter Source: Cotality ‍ High mortgage rates continue to suppress transaction volumes, but severe inventory constraints in the Midwest and Northeast are insulating home prices from broader declines and fueling localized appreciation. Dr. Selma Hepp Cotality Chief Economist Insights from Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp The U.S. housing market modestly reaccelerated in August 2026, with single-family home prices, including distressed sales, rising 1.8% year over year. This is a small increase from the 1.6% annual pace in July and marks the fifth consecutive month of reacceleration. However, August's data largely reflects transactions with mortgage rate lock-ins before the late-August mortgage rate surge. ‍ Although annual price gains have accelerated, the modest monthly decline of 0.1% in August stands in sharp contrast to the pre-pandemic average increase of 0.3% for the month. This continued sluggishness underscores how higher homebuying costs are dampening buyer demand. ‍ Following the sizable increase in mortgage rates since August, the housing market has continued to weaken, with buyer pullback evident in September’s pending home sales. This trend is reflected in the Cotality HPI forecast, which projects month-over-month price declines through the winter and lower annual gains. Overall, annual appreciation for 2026 is expected to reach 1.3%. Beneath this headline figure, however, the real estate landscape remains deeply divided due to persistent rate-lock constraints, shifting migration patterns, and localized inventory imbalances. ‍ The core trend shaping today’s market is the shift away from the once-booming Sunbelt and West Coast cities toward more affordable, inventory-constrained regions in the Midwest and Northeast. Despite a spike in 30-year fixed mortgage rates, buyers continue to seek markets where prices fit traditional debt-to-income ratios. Limited housing supply in these areas is sustaining prices. Conversely, markets with rising inventories, added construction, and slowing job and population growth are still searching for a price bottom. In many of these locations, higher mortgage rates have further discouraged buyers. Overall, the housing market now reflects two distinct realities across the country. ‍ “The national housing market shows a clear split between short-term sensitivity to interest rates and long-term supply shortages,” notes Cotality’s Chief Economist, Dr. Selma Hepp. “High mortgage rates continue to suppress transaction volumes, but severe inventory constraints in the Midwest and Northeast are insulating home prices from broader declines and fueling localized appreciation.” ‍ However, many of the top 100 metropolitan areas are seeing a clear slowdown in 3-month momentum. For example, while San Francisco, CA posted a strong 7.0% year-over-year gain in August 2026, its 3-month momentum turned negative at -2.7%, indicating a sharp late-summer cooldown. ‍ A significant structural divide is persisting between property types. In August 2026, single-family detached homes rose 2.1% year-over-year, while attached properties like condos and townhomes increased by only 0.1%. This widening gap underscores how well-capitalized buyers continue to favor spacious, detached homes, while the condo sector struggles with rising HOA fees, special assessments, and higher insurance premiums. ‍ Geographically, the Midwest and Northeast remain at the forefront of year-over-year price growth. Illinois led all states with a 6.8% annual price gain, trailed by Connecticut (6.3%), Indiana (5.6%), New Jersey (5.6%), and Ohio (4.8%). In these regions, a persistent lack of for-sale listings and limited new construction have fueled competition for available homes, keeping sale prices elevated despite broader economic challenges. ‍ In contrast, major Sunbelt and West Coast markets are grappling with rising inventory and affordability challenges. Texas saw a year-over-year price decline of 0.7%, Washington fell 0.4%, and Hawaii dropped 0.7%. States such as Colorado (+0.1%), Oregon (+0.3%), Arizona (+0.5%), and Nevada (+0.7%) posted nearly flat annual growth. In these regions, increased new-construction completions and buyer resistance to high monthly payments have helped rebuild inventory and ease price pressures. ‍ Over the next 12 months, national home price growth is expected to remain modest, with the Cotality HPI forecasting a 1.7% year-over-year increase by August 2027. State-level projections indicate the Midwest will continue to outperform, while previously overvalued Sunbelt markets are likely to stabilize as mortgage rates gradually decline. ‍ “Looking ahead to 2027, mortgage rates will be the primary driver of home price trends and sales activity. Many buyers halt their searches when rates exceed 7%, but as expectations shift from lower rates in 2027 to ‘higher for longer,’ some may opt to buy rather than keep waiting. Although, elevated rates and ongoing affordability challenges will favor markets with lower entry prices and strong local job growth over former high-growth pandemic hotspots,” says Dr. Hepp. Uncover more Home price indexes Top 10 hottest markets Source: Cotality ‍ Top 10 coolest markets Source: Cotality ‍ Which areas are affordable? items.description: Texas Housing Insight | October 2026 Texas housing activity slowed in August as higher mortgage rates and affordability pressures dampened demand. Inventory remains elevated, prices are stabilizing, and sales may weaken further as rates above 7 percent continue to challenge buyers and sellers. By Yanling Mayer quick links Texas housing market activity slowed in August as the market moved beyond the peak summer selling season and mortgage rates trended higher. Rising Treasury yields and rising inflation pushed mortgage rates upward during the month, impacting buyers already confronting affordability issues. While August's pullback also reflects a typical seasonal cooling, higher financing costs likely amplified the slowdown. Year to date (YTD), sales remain modestly ahead of last year’s, but the lead is expected to narrow in the coming months as mortgage rates have climbed further since August. Statewide, new listing activity largely tracked last year's pace through August, suggesting that homeowners remain willing to enter the market despite slower sales. However, conditions vary across major metropolitan areas. DFW stands out as the weakest large market on the supply side, with new listing volumes remaining soft since April and YTD activity trailing last year's levels. In contrast, seller participation in Austin, Houston, and San Antonio has remained comparatively stable. Active inventory, which expanded steadily throughout the spring and summer, began its normal seasonal decline in August. Even so, inventory levels remain broadly stable and elevated. While some buyers may have been able to take advantage of inventory availability and large seller price concessions, ongoing affordability challenges continue to limit many buyers from fully benefiting from these conditions. Meanwhile, measures such as days on market and inventory turnover suggest that the pace of sales activity remained broadly similar to that of a year ago. Price trends continue to show encouraging signs of stabilization. After more than a year of modest annual declines, statewide home prices were essentially flat in August, breaking a 15-month streak of downward pressures. The moderation in price declines reflects a market that is gradually finding better footing as inventory conditions normalize. Conditions remain somewhat uneven across metros, but overall pricing trends suggest easing downward pricing pressures. Prices in Houston and Fort Worth have trended slightly higher in recent months. Looking ahead, housing activity is likely to remain restrained and could slow further through the remainder of the year. Mortgage rates have climbed back above 7 percent, a threshold that previously weighed heavily on buyers and sellers during the 2023 market downturn. September inflation data suggests overall cost-of-living price pressures remain persistent and rising, raising concerns that interest rates may stay elevated for longer. That means affordability challenges are likely to intensify, creating additional headwinds for home sales and overall housing market activity. items.description: Apartment List National Rent Report By: Chris Salviati and Rob Warnock October 28, 2026 Headline Market Update: November 2026 Year-over-year rent growth in the U.S. flipped positive in October for the first time since mid-2023, though just barely. The national median rent currently stands at $1,384, and is now 0.1% greater than it was at this time last year. The vacancy rate is also gradually tightening, as the market transitions out of the soft conditions that have prevailed in recent years. That said, our newest market indicator tracking the concession rate, continues to show signs of softness. Key Stats National Median Rent: $1,384 per month as of October 2026. Year-Over-Year Rent Growth: Rents are up 0.1% compared to October 2025, marking the first time in over three years that year-over-year rent growth is positive. Month-Over-Month Rent Growth: Rents decreased 0.3% in October 2026 as the rental market enters its off-season; this marks the second consecutive monthly decline. Vacancy Rate: The national multifamily vacancy rate sits at 7% as of October 2026, remaining elevated compared to long-run norms, but continuing to decline after peaking earlier this year. Time on Market: Units are taking an average of 36 days to get leased after being listed, a bit longer than is typical for this time of year. Concessions Rate: 32% of multifamily properties nationally are offering concessions on new leases valued at one month of free rent or greater in October. The concessions rate remains four percentage points higher than at this time last year. Year-over-year rent growth flips positive for first time in over three years For years, the U.S. rental market has been experiencing a prolonged period of sluggishness, as a large wave of multifamily construction had been driving soft pricing and occupancy. However, we’re now at the tail end of that construction boom, and the market has been gradually moving toward more balanced conditions. This month’s data marks a significant milestone in that transition, as year-over-year rent growth flipped positive for the first time in over three years. Following a period of booming rent growth in 2021 and 2022, prices began to cool rapidly, and by June 2023, the national median rent was declining on a year-over-year basis. Full year rent growth was negative for three consecutive years, with prices nationally dipping by -0.8 percent in 2023, by -0.5 percent in 2024, and by -1.2 percent in 2026. Year-over-year rent growth bottomed out at -1.6 percent in April 2026, but over the past six months it has rebounded rapidly as healthy renter demand has filled vacant units and allowed property owners and operators to regain some pricing leverage. Despite the bounceback, rents are still essentially flat compared to one year ago, and are still declining in inflation-adjusted terms. Nonetheless, it’s a significant milestone for the rental market that year-over-year rent growth has now flipped positive. Even as year-year-over rent growth continues to rise, month-over-month rent growth remained negative in October, as the market experiences its typical off-season pricing dip. Fewer renters tend to move in the fall in winter months, and so property owners offer modest discounts to attract demand and fill vacant units at this time of year. But compared to recent years, this year’s fall cooldown has been significantly more subdued. Rents fell by just 0.3 percent in October compared to September; in October of last year, the month-over-month decline was nearly three times as sharp at -0.8 percent. In fact this month’s decline was even slightly more modest than the 2017 to 2019 average (-0.4 percent), a period when the national rental market was in a well-balanced state. In dollar terms, the national median monthly rent now stands at $1,384, up just $1 compared to October 2025. Prices peaked in mid-2022, and have since fallen from that peak by a total of 4 percent, or $58 per month. The national median rent also recently hit a notable milestone – years of modest declines have now offset the rapid price growth that preceded it such that prices are converging back to their long run trend. After oscillating between alternating hot and cool spells throughout the 2020s, the national median rent today is roughly where it would have been if rents had continued to grow at a slow and steady pace of +2.5 percent annually, the average rent growth from 2017 to 2019. This convergence has occurred just as rent growth appears set to stabilize back to something resembling that late-2010s average. Our new concessions rate indicator continues to show some softness This month, in an effort to continue providing actionable, real-time data on the rental market, the Apartment List Economics Team is adding a new dataset to our suite of market indicators: concession rates. Properties that are struggling with occupancy often employ concessions as a strategy for securing new leases. Concessions can take many forms, including discounted rents, cash back offers, gift cards, or free amenities. Such concessions are not factored into our rent estimates, and so tracking them separately provides additional nuance on market conditions. Our published concession rate represents the share of properties offering any discount whose total value is equal to one free month of rent or greater. As of October, 32 percent of all properties are offering concessions valued at one month of free rent or greater. The current concession rate is four percentage points higher than this time last year, when 28 percent of properties were offering such discounts. The concession rate has also ticked up very slightly over the past two months as we enter the off-season.
