items.description: New Home Market Update Zonda tracks 85% of the production new home market across the United States. Given the proprietary database, Zonda is uniquely positioned to capture trends and changes in the new home market. This report showcases the latest housing trends in the new home market for September 2026. October 22, 2026 – 5 min read Table of Content: Pressure builds on the new home market September brought little relief for the new home market: although overall sales rose a modest 1.7% month-over-month, they remained 4.6% below where they stood this time last year. The market showed widespread underperformance despite nearly 40% of builders cutting prices in September, up from 30% in August. Zonda's September builder sentiment survey reinforced the weakness, with 84% of builders reporting slower-than-expected demand, including 60% who said the slowdown was causing concern. Mortgage rates have only added to the pressure, crossing the 7% threshold in late September and climbing further into October. Alongside broader economic uncertainty, higher borrowing costs are making it harder for builders to maintain sales without putting additional pressure on margins. Even when the numbers work, though, buyers may hesitate to make such a significant financial commitment if they're uncertain about their jobs or the broader economy. “The silver lining we’re seeing in the market today is at the high end,” said Ali Wolf, chief economist for Zonda and NewHomeSource. “Prices in the entry-level and move-up/move-down segments declined in September but rose in the high-end market. That doesn’t mean high-end sales are easy. Rather, it reflects that buyers with greater wealth are better positioned to navigate today’s challenging market.” New home sales fell further behind last year Zonda's new home sales metric counts the number of new home contract sales each month and accounts for both cancellations and seasonality. This metric shows there were 690,215 new homes sold in September on a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. This was a gain of 1.7% from last month and a drop of 4.6% from a year ago. On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, 54,334 homes were sold, 4.6% lower than last year and 3.0% above the same month in 2019. Incentives remain a key feature of the new home market, helping to sustain sales activity amid ongoing affordability pressures. In September, 63% of new home communities offered incentives on to-be-built homes and 82% on quick move-in supply. Note, these are only publicly available incentives so will underrepresent overall usage. Pending sales were also subdued Zonda's New Home Pending Sales Index (PSI) was created to help account for fluctuations in supply by combining both total sales volume with the average sales rate per month per community. The September PSI came in at 132.0, representing a 6.0% decline from the same month last year. The index is currently 24.2% below cycle highs. On a month-over-month basis, seasonally adjusted new home sales increased 3.4%. The markets that posted the best numbers relative to last year were Baltimore (+30.3%), New York (+23.2%), and Tampa (+9.7%). Baltimore was up compared to last year and grew 20.4% month-over-month. Inversely, the metros that performed the worst year-over-year were Denver (-40.5%), Washington, DC (-29.0%), and Las Vegas (-17.0%). On a monthly basis, Baltimore, Riverside/San Bernardino, and Los Angeles/OC were the best performing markets. Underperforming markets were widespread In order to add further context to sales, Zonda created the Zonda Market Ranking (ZMR). The ZMR accounts for both sales pace and volume, is seasonally adjusted, and is taken as a percentage relative to a baseline market average. Based on the percentage above or below baseline, markets are bucketed into performance groups ranging from significantly underperforming to significantly overperforming relative to historical activity. The map below shows a snapshot of top production markets by region. Zonda also offers the ZMR for entry-level, move-up/move-down, and high-end markets. Subscribers of the National Outlook report can access all top markets and the tiered breakdown in Zonda’s portal. Non-subscribers can access the tiered maps for the select 10 markets by clicking below. Get ZMR Maps The National ZMR index came in at 95.8 in September, which continued to indicate an average market. Zonda’s snapshot markets were split between 0% overperforming, 30% average, and 70% underperforming. Among Zonda’s top 55 major markets, 14% were overperforming , 33% were average , and 53% were underperforming . Importantly, the ZMR does not account for what it takes to sell a home. For example, securing a sale might still feel difficult in a significantly overperforming market, but if the incentives offered result in a sale, we count the sale. More builders turned to price cuts National home prices increased 2.0% year-over-year for high-end homes to $946,207. Prices fell 2.6% for entry-level to $316,246 and 0.8% for move-up to $513,294. The increase among higher-priced homes reflects a concentration of new communities opening at premium price points, along with larger homesites, bigger floor plans, and more desirable locations. Meanwhile, modest price declines in the entry-level and move-up segments suggest builders continue to prioritize affordability through incentives, product right-sizing, and more competitive pricing in response to softer buyer demand. Supplementing our data with a survey Zonda conducts monthly, 38% of builders lowered prices in September month-over-month, 52% held prices flat, and 10% raised prices. In August, for comparison, 30% of builders lowered prices, 63% held prices flat, and 7% increased prices. Community count up 6.5% from last year There are currently 18,143 actively selling communities tracked by Zonda, up 6.5% year-over-year. On a month-over-month basis, the national figure grew 0.8%.                     FHFA House Price Index® Up 0.3 Percent in August;
                            Up 2.4 Percent from Last Year
Washington, D.C. – U.S. house prices rose nationwide in August, up 0.3 percent from the previous
month, according to the U.S. Federal Housing (FHFA) seasonally adjusted monthly House Price
Index (FHFA HPI®). House prices rose 2.4 percent from August 2025 to August 2026. The
previously reported 0.3 percent price increase in July was revised down to 0.2 percent.

For the nine census divisions, seasonally adjusted monthly home price changes ranged from -0.8
percent in the New England division to +2.1 percent in the East South Central division. The 12-
month changes ranged from +0.5 percent in the Mountain division to +4.4 percent in the East North
Central division.

The FHFA HPI is a comprehensive collection of publicly available house price indexes that tracks
changes in single-family home values across the United States. The data extend back to the mid-1970s
and cover all 50 states and more than 400 American cities. Drawing on information from over 100
million home sales and refinance transactions, the FHFA HPI provides detailed insights into house price
trends at the national, census division, state, metropolitan area, county, ZIP code, and census tract
levels. FHFA employs a transparent, weighted repeat-sales methodology to measure changes in home
prices using historical housing transaction data.

FHFA releases HPI data and reports quarterly and monthly. The flagship FHFA HPI uses seasonally
adjusted, purchase-only data from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Additional indexes use other data,
including refinances, mortgages insured by the Federal Housing Administration, and real property
records. All the indexes (including their historic values) and information about future HPI release dates
are available on FHFA’s website: https://www.fhfa.gov/HPI.

The next HPI report will be released on November 24, 2026, and will include monthly data through
September 2026 and quarterly data through the third quarter of 2026.

    The Federal Housing Finance Agency regulates Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the 11 Federal Home Loan Banks. These

items.title: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter
items.description: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter by ATTOM Team | Oct 29, 2026 | Foreclosures , Real Estate News - Recent Articles The national vacancy rate declined to 1.2 percent; Zombie home rate dropped slightly to 3 percent IRVINE, Calif. – October 29, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, the leading provider of property data , AI-powered analytics, and real estate intelligence solutions, today released its latest Vacant Property and Zombie Foreclosure Report showing that 1.2 percent of residential properties in the United States were vacant in the final quarter of the year. That was down from 1.3 percent in the third quarter and in the same quarter last year. The report analyzes publicly recorded real estate data collected by ATTOM — including foreclosure status, equity and owner-occupancy status — matched against monthly updated vacancy data. (See full methodology below). There were 269,195 properties in the foreclosure process in the fourth quarter, out of 105.1 million total properties analyzed. Of those properties in foreclosure, 3 percent, or 8,040 properties, were “zombies,” meaning the owners had abandoned the homes before the conclusion of the foreclosure proceedings. The fourth-quarter zombie rate was down from 3.3 percent in the prior quarter and in the same quarter last year. “The fourth-quarter data showed modest declines in both vacancy and zombie foreclosure rates nationwide,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “While trends vary from state to state, vacant and abandoned homes continue to represent a relatively small share of the nation’s housing stock.” Zombie homes on rise in majority of states The number of zombie properties rose quarter-over-quarter in 29 states. Among states with at least 50 zombie properties in the fourth quarter, the largest quarter-over-quarter increases were in Wisconsin (up 20.9 percent to 52 zombie properties), Maryland (up 19.2 percent to 180 zombie properties), Pennsylvania (up 17.2 percent to 252 zombie properties), Texas (up 15.7 percent to 192 zombie properties), and North Carolina (up 15.2 percent to 129 zombie properties). The states with sufficient data to analyze and that had the largest declines in zombie properties were Arizona (down 34.9 percent to 56 zombie properties), Florida (down 19.6 percent to 2,220 zombie properties), California (down 10.4 percent to 267 zombie properties), South Carolina (down 9.6 percent to 141 zombie properties), and Oklahoma (down 8.9 percent to 82 zombie properties). Vacancy rates below half a percent in much of Northeast The states with the highest overall home vacancy rates in the fourth quarter were Oklahoma (2.4 percent), Kansas (2.3 percent), Alabama (2.1 percent), West Virginia (2.1 percent), and Missouri (2 percent). The lowest vacancy rates were in New Hampshire (0.3 percent), Vermont (0.4 percent), New Jersey (0.4 percent), Connecticut (0.4 percent), and Idaho (0.5 percent). Ten metro areas posted no zombie properties There were 164 metropolitan statistical areas with sufficient data to include in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 100,000 residential properties and at least 50 properties in the foreclosure process. The metro areas with the highest zombie rates were Baltimore, MD (13 percent); Youngstown, OH (13 percent); Akron, OH (11.5 percent); Cedar Rapids, IA (10.7 percent); and Scranton, PA (9.4 percent). Ten of the metro areas had no zombie properties, the largest of which were Bridgeport, CT; El Paso, TX; Little Rock, AR; Fayetteville, AR; and Visalia, CA. Vacancy rates higher among investor-owned properties Institutional investors held 30.6 million homes in the fourth quarter, of which 2.7 percent, or 840,384, were vacant. The states with the highest vacancy rates for investor-owned homes were Indiana (6.5 percent), Alabama (5.8 percent), Oklahoma (5.4 percent), Kansas (5.2 percent), and Louisiana (5.1 percent). The lowest vacancy rates for investor-owned properties were in New Hampshire (0.6 percent), Vermont (0.9 percent), Utah (0.9 percent), Hawaii (1 percent), and New Jersey (1.1 percent). Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Zombie rates high in several Baltimore, Indianapolis zip codes There were 2,585 zip codes with sufficient data to be included in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 1,000 residential properties and at least 25 in foreclosure in the fourth quarter. Of those, the highest zombie rates were in 21205 in Baltimore, MD (42.5 percent); 21223 in Baltimore, MD (40 percent); 46201 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); 46218 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); and 13619 in Carthage, NY (32.1 percent). Conclusion ATTOM’s fourth quarter vacancy and zombie home report found that the national vacancy rate fell slightly from the previous quarter to 1.2 percent. The national zombie home rate also dropped to 3 percent. Report Methodology ATTOM analyzed county tax assessor data for over 105.1 million residential properties for vacancy, broken down by foreclosure status and owner-occupancy status in the fourth quarter of 2026. items.description: Realpage Economy Express Episode 73 by Arben Skivjani Posted October 19, 2026 in Insights Hotter-than-expected September inflation readings at both the consumer and wholesale level have strengthened the case for a second Fed rate hike ahead of the late October meeting. The consumer price report showed prices rose 0.6% in September, lifting the annual rate to 3.7%, the highest since May. Core inflation also picked up to 2.6%, with airfares, used cars, medical care and apparel all moving higher. According to the producer price report, wholesale prices jumped 1.3% in a single month, the biggest gain since early 2022, and were up 6.3% from a year ago. Goods prices alone rose 2.6%, the most since the series began in 2009. Minutes from the Fed's September meeting reveal that every official backed the rate hike and most expect another by year-end. The Fed's Beige Book found prices rising fast in three districts and accelerating in four. Markets now see another hike by December as very likely and put a 1-in-4 chance on two more. Retail sales data for September showed a 0.8% increase, but with prices up 0.6%, most of that gain reflects higher prices rather than more purchases. Weekly jobless claims, at 199,000, show the labor market is still holding up even as consumer sentiment sits at its lowest since May's record low. Mortgage rates have climbed to 7.5%, the highest since late 2023, according to mortgage market data, while existing home sales stayed under 4 million. For more information on the state of the U.S. Economy, including forecasts, watch all the episodes of the Economy Express series. items.description: Mortgage Rates Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® (PMMS ® ) results are based on the mortgage rate collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac through Loan Product Advisor ® (LPA ® ) from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. Learn more in our FAQs . Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® U.S. weekly mortgage rate averages as of 10/29/2026 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 7.24% 15-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 6.60% Download Rates Since 1971 Mortgage Rates Decline Further to 7.24% The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage declined again this week, reaching its lowest level this month and modestly boosting purchasing power for prospective buyers. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.24% as of October 29, 2026, down from last week when it averaged 7.32%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.17%. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.60%, down from last week when it averaged 6.68%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.41%. PMMS results are released weekly on Thursdays at 12 p.m. ET. and are an average of loan rates offered the prior Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . items.title: Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter
items.description: Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter October 30, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Private fixed investment in student dormitories rose 2.6% in the third quarter of 2026, reaching a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of $3.8 billion. This gain marked a second consecutive quarterly increase, despite continued pressures from elevated interest rates. On a year-over-year basis, investments in dorms increased 1.1%. Private fixed investment in student housing experienced a surge after the Great Recession, as college enrollment increased from 17.2 million in 2006 to 20.4 million in 2011. However, during the pandemic, private fixed investment in student housing declined drastically from $4.4 billion (SAAR) in the last quarter of 2019 to $3.1 billion in the second quarter of 2021. According to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center , college enrollment fell by 3.6% in the fall of 2020 and by 3.1% in the fall of 2021. The latest preliminary data indicated that college enrollment held steady in fall 2026 compared with the previous year. Since the pandemic, private fixed investment in dorms has rebounded alongside a gradual recovery in college enrollments. Effective in-person learning requires college students to return to campuses, boosting the student housing sector. Still, demographic trends are reshaping the outlook for student housing. The U.S. faces slower growth in the college-age population as birth rates declined following the Great Recession. Furthermore, changing perceptions towards the value of a college degree as a guaranteed pathway to job security are all contributing to an “enrollment cliff”. items.description: September 2026 Central Texas Housing Report 10/13/2026 Central Texas housing market adjusts amid challenging economic conditions 2026-Q3 sales dip 2.4% year over year AUSTIN, Texas — According to the September and 2026-Q3 Central Texas Housing Report released by Unlock MLS , rising mortgage rates weighed on the Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos MSA housing market in September, slowing sales activity as higher monthly payments created additional affordability challenges for buyers. Closed sales declined 14.8% year over year to 2,223 sales, while the median sales price increased 1.4% to $421,000. Pending sales declined just 1.8% to 2,313, suggesting some buyers remained engaged despite higher borrowing costs. Homes also closed at an average of 92.7% of their original list price, compared to 91.4% a year earlier, reflecting closer alignment between buyers and sellers in closed transactions. While September's sharper decline highlights the immediate pressure of rising rates, third-quarter figures provide a broader view of market activity, with closed sales declining 2.4% year over year to 7,748 and the median sales price decreasing 2.3% to $420,000. Vaike O’Grady , research advisor at Unlock MLS, said September’s slowdown reflects a shift in market activity following the recent increase in mortgage rates. “September's decline in closed sales is significant, and it shows just how sensitive today's housing market is to changes in mortgage rates. We had been seeing steady activity, but the recent increase in rates created another hurdle for buyers, especially those trying to enter the market for the first time. The biggest factor for many buyers isn't necessarily the price of the home, but what that price means for their monthly payment at today's rates. While affordability remains a real challenge, we're still seeing activity in the market. The question now is how buyers and sellers respond to these conditions in the months ahead.” John Crowe , 2026 Unlock MLS and ABoR president, emphasized the importance of understanding local market conditions and working with a real estate professional when making buying or selling decisions. “It's easy to look at a headline about declining sales or rising mortgage rates and feel discouraged, but every buyer and seller is in a different position. What's happening across the broader market may look very different depending on the neighborhood, price point or type of home you're considering. That's where working with a knowledgeable real estate agent can make a real difference. items.title: U.S. Pending Home Sales Sink to a New Low
items.description: U.S. Pending Home Sales Sink to a New Low Published on October 22nd, 2026 by Dana Anderson Would-be homebuyers are pulling back as mortgage rates remain in the mid-7% range. What to know about the U.S. housing market for the four weeks ending October 18: Pending home sales fell. They declined 1.9% from a week earlier to the lowest level in records dating back to 2021 . Weekly average mortgage rates are holding steady at 7.4% , pricing out many house hunters. For the second week in a row, pending sales declined in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metro areas. The typical monthly payment jumped to the the second-highest level on record. The median housing payment for a homebuyer is $2,796, as mortgage rates stay high. But the median home-sale price rose just 0.2% year over year, following two weeks of 0.1% increases, a sign that prices are losing steam. Fresh supply is falling. New listings declined 1.4% from a week earlier to the lowest level since July as homeowners take note of slow homebuying demand. Total inventory is still growing–but barely. The total number of homes for sale inched up 0.1% week over week; even though new listings are falling, the total number of homes for sale is holding up because buyers aren’t depleting the pool very quickly. There are hundreds of thousands more home sellers than buyers throughout the country, giving buyers the most negotiating power they’ve had in over a decade. items.title: U.S. Industrial Market Outlook – September 2026
items.description: Industrial Market Real Estate Trends U.S. Industrial Market Outlook – September 2026 Diana Firtea October 5, 2026 2 Min Read Image by Roman Vyshnikov/iStock Industrial fundamentals continued to rebalance in August, while renewed construction activity and record e-commerce penetration pointed to durable long-term logistics demand, the latest Yardi Matrix Industrial National Report shows. Report highlights In-place rents averaged $9.31 per square foot, up 5.4 percent year over year National vacancy held at 9.3 percent, up 60 basis points annually Leases signed during the past 12 months averaged $10.19 per square foot 446.9 million square feet of industrial space was under construction, equal to 2.1 percent of stock Industrial sales totaled $60.5 billion through August at $138 per square foot Leasing conditions remain uneven Rent growth remained strongest in several Sun Belt and East Coast markets. Atlanta led major metros with a 7.9 percent annual increase, followed by New Jersey and Miami at 7.6 percent and Dallas at 7.5 percent. Higher-priced coastal markets included Orange County at $18.09 per square foot, Los Angeles at $15.97 and the Bay Area at $15.29. The national spread between new and in-place leases continued to compress. Newly signed leases averaged $10.19 per square foot, just $0.88 above the $9.31 in-place average. Bridgeport retained the widest premium at $3.52, followed by Boston at $3.02 and Miami at $2.97. Seattle moved in the opposite direction of the strongest rent-growth markets. Its vacancy rate reached 13.6 percent after rising 500 basis points in two years, reflecting the absorption challenge created by 44.2 million square feet delivered since the start of 2020. Large projects reshape the pipeline Industrial construction reached 446.9 million square feet nationally. Dallas led in absolute volume with 37.3 million square feet underway, followed by Phoenix with 31.1 million and Houston with 21.8 million. Phoenix had the largest pipeline relative to existing inventory at 6.8 percent of stock, with another 7.2 percent planned. Large-format development is becoming increasingly important. Forty-nine projects exceeding 1 million square feet broke ground through August, and facilities of that scale accounted for more than 32 percent of all 2026 starts by square footage. Demand is also receiving support from e-commerce, which reached a record 20.2 percent of core retail sales in the second quarter. Meanwhile, industrial transactions totaled $60.5 billion through August. Dallas recorded the most sales at $4.1 billion, while Los Angeles averaged $297 per square foot and Memphis averaged $75, illustrating the wide dispersion in pricing nationally. items.title: Beyond the Rent: What is the true cost of your equity?
items.description: Beyond the Rent: What is the true cost of your equity? Many owners face the challenge of bringing more money into their deal. Sometimes, the cost may outweigh the benefits. Published Oct. 30, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Beyond the Rent is Multifamily Dive’s analysis of the trends driving supply, demand and operations in the apartment industry. You can read the previous edition here . These days, it feels like you can find a stat to support just about anything you want. Think inflation isn’t an issue? If you watch the Sunday political shows long enough, someone probably has numbers to support that notion. On the other side, there’s probably someone who can tell you that the third-quarter U.S. real gross domestic product growth of 3.4% is a mirage. Think Brian Schottenheimer isn’t getting enough out of the Dallas Cowboys? (Spoiler alert: he isn’t, despite this week's win.) The folks at Pro Football Focus probably have something to back those claims. The same is true in multifamily. Since I started covering this sector, the number of studies, surveys and indexes that fill my inbox each day seems to have quadrupled … at least. I delete most of these research projects or studies because much of this “research” is sent under the guise of pitching products. However, I do look at certain reports and even seek others out. As more loans face issues in the apartment industry, I recently went to CRED iQ’s website to get an idea of the size of the maturity wall. There I found something that caught my eye — an article saying nearly 33% of maturing apartment debt needs a cash infusion to refinance. At first blush, that number felt, well, kind of low, given everything that I’ve been reading about maturity walls and refinance risk. Reading further on the CRED iQ website, I learned that the firm resized every multifamily loan in Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and commercial mortgage-backed securities deals maturing between October 2026 and December 2028. Of that $136 billion in debt, 23% of the loans and 31% of the balance can’t refinance without an equity infusion of roughly $6.8 billion. The good news for apartment owners is that money is available to fill that gap. The bad news: It’s getting more expensive. Earlier this year, Maximiliane Leachman, vice chair of CBRE’s debt and structured finance group, told me refinancing is becoming harder for some borrowers. At one point, these lenders may have wanted 1% to 3% of the loan balance for an extension. Now, many could be looking for 10%. “We’re all waiting for the shoe to drop at the end of this year as those borrowers come back for the second time to that debt fund for another modification,” Leachman said. “It will be interesting to see how many of those go back.” But costs aren’t the only issues owners must weigh when deciding whether to bring additional capital into their deals. In a recent conversation, Michael Lynd, CEO of Kairoi Residential, raised another concern: whether refinancing is worth the cost to existing equity holders. “The question that I have when I look at a lot of these refinances is the cost of that refinance is not great for your existing equity,” Lynd said. “If rent growth doesn’t show up in that first six to nine months or a year, then you have a chance of further impairing the equity value that isn't in place.” Lynd thinks a lot of groups are making decisions that might not be in their investors’ best interests by holding on to properties rather than selling them because they don’t want a negative trade on their record. Alternatively, they may want to delay a sale to raise additional capital. “I see it happening all over the place,” Lynd said. “You can get a loan, but should you take that loan? Is that the best risk-adjusted decision for your equity?” If the answer is no and if the market doesn’t snap back, those firms might be doing their investors a disservice. Still, some owners may find data showing refinancing is the best option. And it could be. But just because you can find the data to say something doesn’t make it so. These properties are now eligible for Federal Housing Administration-insurance under two multifamily programs: Section 221(d)(4) for new construction and Section 223(f) for acquisition or refinancing of recently developed rental communities. "In theory, this announcement will lower the cost of capital for BTR by providing more stable and cheaper financing options," said Thom Malone, principal economist for Cotality. "This would increase the supply of rental housing, which would put downward pressure on rents, but that would be blunted since it would also increase demand by making more families choose renting over buying." However, Malone thinks the effects would be extremely small, possibly not even detectable in practice. "Even if the cost of capital is lower, it does not alter real-world bottlenecks like processing delays and restrictive local zoning," Malone continued. BTR is not a large part of the market, he said, with the number of starts totalling fewer than 100,000 a year. "Even if this program increased that by 20%, that would still mean only 15,000 to 20,000 more rental units — a drop in the bucket of the U.S. rental market," Malone said. Still, this change not only helps those who need this type of financing but also gives lenders another product they can offer at a time when industry economists are expecting owner-occupied residential volume to decline 5% in 2027. As long as the Fed keeps rates elevated, consumers are unlikely to see much relief from the high prices and higher borrowing costs that continue to weigh on household budgets. watch now VIDEO 5:49 05:49 Barclays' Giannoni sees Fed hiking in Dec and Jan as inflation pressures persist Squawk Box Asia The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, even as rising energy costs threaten to keep inflation elevated and further strain already-tight household budgets. Higher energy prices stemming from the Iran war may prove stickier than expected, but the central bank's decision to hold rates steady gives policymakers more time to assess the economic fallout. The dynamic could also lead Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee to consider raising rates at their December meeting in order to bring inflation down to the Fed's 2% target. For now, however, persistent inflation and higher borrowing costs are compounding affordability challenges for many households, economists say. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, said in a post on Oct. 12 that the war has cost the average American household about $2,000 so far, mostly due to higher energy costs, in addition to heightened interest rate costs. "High-net-worth consumers are enjoying the runup in AI stocks and the value of their equity holdings, and are spending with some gusto," Zandi told CNBC. "Lower- and middle-income consumers are increasingly struggling with falling real wages and high rates, and are much more cautious and careful spenders." How the Fed impacts your money The Federal Reserve's decision to keep rates at the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, and the expectation that more rate increases are in the pipeline, means consumers are unlikely to see much relief from high borrowing costs anytime soon. The Fed influences the federal funds rate, an interest rate benchmark that sets what banks charge each other for overnight lending. That rate ripples throughout the economy, influencing both consumer borrowing costs and returns on savings. Short-term consumer lending rates, such as credit cards, closely track the prime rate, which typically moves in tandem with the Fed's benchmark and is generally about 3 percentage points higher. Longer-term rates, like those on 30-year mortgages, meanwhile, are driven more by inflation expectations and the economic outlook. Columbia Commercial Litigation Attorney Senior Attorney - Arizona or New Mexico Explore More Job Openings HB Ad Slot PE Ownership of Single-Family Rentals: The Legislative Landscape (Part 1) by: Brian Boland , Darrow Everett LLP Monday, October 5, 2026 Related Practices Jurisdictions Real Estate Mergers Acquisitions Communications Media Internet Administrative Regulatory All Federal Print Mail Download />i Editor’s note: This is Part 1 of a two-part series on PE ownership of single-family rentals. Part 2 covers enforcement under existing law and the tax and structuring risks the return model may miss. Legislators in statehouses across the country have spent the last several sessions introducing bills to cap how many single-family homes an investment entity may own. Few have become law. Regulators and private plaintiffs have also secured substantial settlements from the sector’s largest operators over pricing, fee disclosures, and security-deposit practices. The key point for sponsors is the gap between political attention and where money is actually leaving the business. The sector’s origins still shape its regulation. After 2008, investors bought distressed homes in bulk. The business has since become an institutional asset class, with dedicated funds, purpose-built management platforms, securitized debt, and build-to-rent pipelines. State legislatures and campaigns now use it as shorthand for the broader U.S. housing-affordability crisis. This DE Insight is for sponsors and their counsel. It explains where the law is moving, which exposures already create liability, and how to respond. The short version: monitor ownership-cap bills, but existing consumer-protection, antitrust, and fair-housing laws pose the more immediate risk to platform-scale operations. The Investment Case for Institutional Single-Family Rentals The investment thesis is straightforward. For more than a decade, the number of new households looking for a place to live has grown faster than new single-family construction. Entitlement delays, scarce lots, labor constraints, and material costs have kept new supply below trend. More households want detached homes with more space and better schools but cannot or do not want to buy. Higher mortgage rates and down-payment requirements have pushed monthly ownership costs above monthly rent in many markets. Institutional capital brought scale to a fragmented ownership base. It centralized maintenance, standardized leasing, funded deferred repairs, and, through build-to-rent, financed construction that a fragmented buyer pool might not support. Those investments add housing and can improve housing quality. Sponsors should be ready to document that value. Scale, Concentration, and the Data Problem The national numbers are smaller than the rhetoric suggests. Institutional investors own only a small share of the country’s single-family rentals. Individuals and small landlords still own most rental homes. But measuring institutional ownership is hard: homes sit behind layers of entities, and public records rarely show the ultimate owner. The national figure misses what legislators see on the ground. Institutional buying has focused on a limited number of high-growth Sun Belt metros and, within those markets, on particular neighborhoods and price ranges. Reported purchase shares in those areas were well above the national average and higher still in some neighborhoods. Local buyers, brokers, and officials see that concentration; they do not see the national percentage. items.title: UK Budget Risks Deterring Sovereign Wealth Funds From Real Estate
items.description: The budget is out, and the property industry has concerns. UK Chancellor John Healey avoided a bond-market shock with his “breathing space” budget , and the immediate financial-market reaction was reassuring. Gilt yields did not spike, avoiding an outcome that could have pushed financing costs up even further. However, investors were left waiting for measures capable of bringing borrowing costs down and stimulating new development. The budget also delivered limited progress on development viability, while business rates measures offered some relief to high street occupiers without delivering the structural reform sought by many property owners. But new proposed tax rules for sovereign investors, which threaten to make the UK less attractive to global property capital, caused a sharp intake of breath. Flickr/House of Commons Chancellor John Healey succeeded in placating bond markets, but the property sector raised concerns over sovereign taxes. The government has launched a consultation over its proposal to replace the largely noncodified sovereign immunity from direct taxation with a statutory regime from 1 January 2029. Certain UK property income and capital gains would become taxable, although the reforms include bespoke access to the real estate investment trust regime, with a 15% tax rate on qualifying property income distributions. State-operated overseas pension funds and certain investment management activities would remain exempt. The government claimed the reforms would improve transparency and provide greater certainty for sovereign investors, but many in the property industry worry it could weaken the UK's appeal to investors. “It’s a really unhelpful change,” Real Estate:UK Assistant Director of Finance Rachel Kelly said. She said the proposal introduces additional costs for a significant source of real estate investment while development viability is already under severe pressure. Sovereign wealth funds invested £6.2B in UK property from 2021 to 2024, according to a March report from BPF and CoStar . Although the proposed REIT arrangements and transitional provisions offer some flexibility, the new 15% rate would be a significant increase for qualifying sovereign investors accustomed to paying no tax. It also adds an onerous process. “In addition to the actual additional cost now of investing in the UK for those investors, there will be huge complexity in terms of having to restructure their investments, and there will be a lot of work for some to change how they're structured,” Kelly said. The implications extend beyond the funds themselves. Sovereign wealth funds frequently invest alongside other capital providers, meaning changes to their investment structures could affect co-investors and joint ventures too, Moorfield CEO Charles Ferguson-Davie said. He said the reforms risk sending the wrong signal. “There aren’t that many groups that will deploy over £500M, over a billion,” Ferguson-Davie said. “If they’re going to be less active as a result of having to pay tax, who’s going to step in and invest that money instead?” CBRE Investment Management is looking to understand the rules in more detail during the consultation, Director Alex Lund said. But he expressed optimism that the policy won’t decimate investment. “For any market looking to attract overseas capital ... taxes and the need for a level playing field for domestic and international investors are very important,” he said. “But many investors are already in the UK, which is a large, deep and transparent market, so we would remain positive while looking at the consultation carefully.” Ferguson-Davie said the wider economic benefits of attracting large-scale investment should be part of the government's calculations, rather than focusing solely on the tax revenue generated. He said the string of regulatory or tax burdens added to the private rental sector over the last few budgets show the danger in the government’s thinking. “You can understand the political motivation, but it has already led to a lot of sales and exits from the market,” Ferguson-Davie said. “I'm not sure it's all necessarily ending up benefiting the renter.” Instead, supply and development have both fallen, and that pushes rents up. He said the new budget will encourage the sale of buy-to-lets, which could benefit the institutional build-to-rent sector — but it doesn’t actually solve any problems. “What the BTR community needs, indeed the housing sector needs, is more incentives to help bring down the cost of development,” he said. “If we're going to have a meaningful change in terms of new houses delivered for sale and for rent, we need the regulatory and tax burden reduced, because otherwise it's just going to get worse.” BTR construction starts have fallen 63% in the last year, with only 4,696 groundbreakings in September, versus 12,674 the year prior, according to Savills data for RE:UK . “Investors needed more than a pause in policy changes,” Kelly said. The budget's business rates package provided more immediate support for retail, hospitality and leisure businesses. However, Kelly said the chancellor again failed to deliver meaningful long-term reform. While the absence of another proposed surcharge on higher-value commercial property was welcome, RE:UK has called for the existing surcharge to be repealed and the tax system changed to make investment and refurbishment more attractive. Unsplash/Daniel Bond markets remained stable after the "breathing space" budget. The budget’s impact on London will be mixed, Knight Frank partner and Head of London Research Shabab Qadar said in a statement. The temporary increase in the bank surcharge could dampen a tenant pool that drives London’s global competitiveness, he said. items.title: Case-Shiller: Phoenix home-price growth increases in August
items.description: Case-Shiller: Phoenix home-price growth increases in August by John Yellig October 27, 2026 The pace of home-price growth across the United States continued to accelerate in August despite varying widely between markets. No. 1 Chicago saw prices jump, while lowest-ranked Seattle saw a decline. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index rose 2.1% year over year in August, up from a 1.9% gain in July. Month over month, the index slipped 0.02%. S&P Dow Jones noted that home values actually fell in real terms for the 15th month in a row, as August's 3.4% inflation erased the 2.1% gain in prices. “U.S. home prices declined in real terms for the 15th consecutive month in August 2026, though the gap narrowed as nominal home price growth strengthened,” said Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices. "Affordability, however, remains challenging. With inflation at 3.4%, Brent crude near $100 per barrel and mortgage rates in the mid-to-high 6% range, households continue to face elevated costs alongside persistently high home prices.” In Phoenix, home prices inched 0.42% higher year over year and slipped 0.53% month over month in August. items.title: Pretium Expands Middle East Presence with Abu Dhabi Office
items.description: Pretium Expands Middle East Presence with Abu Dhabi Office October 14, 2026 --> Office will enable Pretium to engage more directly with institutional partners across the Middle East NEW YORK and ABU DHABI, October 14, 2026 – Pretium, a specialized investment firm with approximately $70 billion in assets under management [1] , today announced the opening of an office in Abu Dhabi. The office will operate within Abu Dhabi Global Market (“ADGM”), the international financial center of Abu Dhabi, providing proximity to some of the world’s leading institutional investors. The Abu Dhabi office marks an important step in the continued evolution of Pretium’s business. From its roots in U.S. residential real estate, Pretium has built a scaled investment platform spanning real estate equity and credit. A dedicated presence in Abu Dhabi will enhance the Firm’s connections to clients in the region as it continues to develop new investment solutions. “Abu Dhabi is home to some of the world’s most sophisticated and forward-looking institutional investors,” said Don Mullen, Founder and CEO of Pretium. “An on-the-ground presence here will enable us to spend more time alongside our partners in the region and help expand their investment opportunities through Pretium’s vertically integrated residential real estate ecosystem.” “Pretium’s decision to establish a presence in Abu Dhabi reflects the continued growth and global appeal of the capital’s financial ecosystem. As leading investment firms expand closer to regional institutional partners, ADGM provides a trusted, internationally recognised platform from which they can build meaningful relationships, unlock new opportunities and contribute to Abu Dhabi’s position as a leading global financial centre,” said Arvind Ramamurthy, Chief Market Development Officer at ADGM. The office will be located in ADGM and led by Basim Habib, Director in Business Development, and Dietrich Heidtmann, Managing Director in Business Development, who will work closely with Pretium teams across the Firm. About Pretium Pretium is a specialized investment firm focused on U.S. residential real estate equity and credit. Pretium was founded in 2012 and has built an integrated analytical and operational ecosystem within the U.S. housing and credit markets and believes that its insight and experience within these markets create a strategic advantage. Pretium’s platform has approximately $70 billion in assets and employs 7,000 people across 45+ offices, including its New York headquarters, Miami, London, Abu Dhabi, Bangalore, Seoul and Sydney. Please visit www.pretium.com for additional information. Media Contact Brenna Karp Pretium [email protected] [1] As of June 30, 2026

items.description: Share: Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn I recommend visiting cushmanwakefield.com to read:%0A%0A {0} %0A%0A {1} Insights U.S. Industrial Reports With logistics playing a critical role in business strategy, understanding the industrial market is essential. Explore key trends in our latest MarketBeat report, including supply, demand, and pricing. DOWNLOAD Q3 2026 REPORT Key INDUSTRIAL Takeaways For Q3 2026 Quarterly net absorption reached 76.6 million square feet (msf), its highest level since Q1 2023. Demand surpassed 70 msf for the second consecutive quarter, bringing the year-to-date (YTD) total to 203 msf, the strongest three-quarter stretch since late 2022. New industrial supply remained modest in Q3 2026, with 64 msf delivered nationwide. Completions YTD are 13% behind last year's pace. The national industrial vacancy rate fell 20 basis points (bps) from year-end 2025 to 6.8%, its lowest level since year-end 2024. Developer confidence is returning as demand strengthens and vacancy stabilizes. The under-construction pipeline increased 23% year-over-year (YOY) to 324 msf, its highest level since mid-2024. For the data behind the commentary, download the full Q3 2026 U.S. Industrial Report. Despite Economic Uncertainties, Industrial Demand Accelerates Net absorption accelerated to 76.6 msf in Q3, its strongest quarter since Q1 2023. Demand exceeded 70 msf for a second consecutive quarter, lifting the YTD total to 203 msf, 69% higher than the first three quarters of 2025. Inland markets are driving activity, accounting for 80% of YTD absorption. Port markets are also improving, with YTD demand already surpassing the full-year 2025 total, led by third-quarter surges in Houston, New Jersey, the Inland Empire, Savannah and Miami. Newer product continues to attract the strongest demand, with 202 msf of YTD net absorption in warehouses built this decade. However, as availability in newer facilities tightens, demand is beginning to spill over into older properties. Warehouses built from 2000 through 2019, which experienced steady occupancy losses over the previous two years, are now showing signs of stabilization. New leasing YTD is 21% above last year's pace. The surge in AI buildouts, resilient consumer spending, and nearshoring and onshoring has propelled leasing activity to its strongest six-month period in more than four years. Demand has been led by 3PL, manufacturing, e-commerce and data center-related tenants. Manufacturers remained the second most active tenant type through the first three quarters of 2026 as they continue to build out and evolve their supply chains nationwide. After accounting for 23% of annual leasing volume the previous three years, manufacturing companies represented more than one-fourth of YTD 2026 activity. Tenants looking for large format warehouses have been particularly active, with transactions above 500,000 sf making up more than one-third of YTD leasing volume. Nationwide Vacancy Drifts Further Below Its Recent Peak With demand outpacing new supply for two straight quarters, U.S. industrial vacancy has fallen 20 bps from its late-2025 peak of 7%. At 6.8%, the rate is at its lowest point since year-end 2024 and is expected to decline modestly by the end of 2026. Vacancy fell by 100 bps or more YOY in 14 U.S. markets, including Indianapolis, Columbus, Phoenix, Central Valley and Philadelphia. Larger facilities have led the compression. Vacancy in buildings of 500,000 sf or more fell 280 bps YOY to 7.4%, while the mid-sized segment (300,000--500,000 sf) is also stabilizing, with vacancy down 50 bps. Asking rental rate growth reached 4% nationwide in Q3, up from roughly 1% during the second half of 2025 and marking the third consecutive quarter of acceleration. Strong gains in the South and Midwest contributed. Of the 83 markets tracked, 13 reported double-digit YOY growth in Q3, led by Dallas-Fort Worth at 20%. St. Louis, Louisville, Tampa, Raleigh-Durham and Indianapolis all posted annual rent growth above 10%. Conversely, rents continued to soften in some key coastal markets in California, New Jersey and Miami. New Deliveries Remain Modest, But the Pipeline Is Expanding New supply remained modest, with nearly 64 msf of completions in Q3. The YTD total of 185 msf is down 13% YOY. Texas accounted for one-fourth of U.S. deliveries in 2026 (47 msf), while five other inland markets each recorded more than 5 msf of completions: the PA I-81/I-78 Corridor, Chicago, Atlanta, Phoenix and Louisville. In some smaller markets, including El Paso, Fredericksburg, Boise and Raleigh-Durham, YTD completions equal more than 3% of their current inventories. As leasing activity strengthens and vacancy stabilizes, developers are growing more confident. The pipeline rose 23% YOY to 324 msf, its highest level since mid-2024. Pipelines grew YOY in half of U.S. markets, including 14 with gains of more than 100%. Build-to-suit projects make up about 35% of the overall pipeline and more than 55% of the large-format pipeline (500,000 sf or more), as large logistics tenants seek customized facilities for long-term needs. items.title: A path to sub-7% mortgage rates is back on the table
items.description: Housing demand has stabilized over the last two weeks as rates have fallen a tad, and we can finally see a clear path back to sub-7% mortgage rates . We survived the crazy month of October, when the 10-year had the potential to close above 5.35%, which would have created a backdrop of bond-escalation selling, sending mortgage rates above 8%. That didn’t happen, of course, as the 10-year yield held that key line! Not only has the 10-year yield now gone below 5% — with mortgage rates closer to 7% than 8% today — but what this month has shown us is that there’s a clear path for sub-7% mortgage rates. Just the move in the last two weeks has stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, so let’s take a look on this Halloween on what needs to happen to get rates lower. 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% Last week was Fed week, and even Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said tighter policy has created financial pain for some AI companies. The Federal Reserve has been talking more and more about AI being very inflationary for many weeks now, so naturally, when AI companies are having debt-financing issues, and some are missing on their numbers, the 10-year yield has gone lower even with elevated oil prices and economic data staying firm. However, imagine for a minute that the Iran conflict was over: oil would be trading between $67 and $82. Imagine that the trade war 2.0 doesn’t get worse and you have an AI slowdown; there’s your trinity for lower mortgage rates. Nothing too drastic, but definitely sub-7%, and we’ve all seen what mortgage demand can do when rates drop below 6.64%. So there’s a pathway to 7%, but there’s also a pathway for rates to stay above 7% if the AI story rebounds, the conflict doesn’t end, and the trade war continues. This, of course, would need the economic data to stay very positive, as it has recently. Since Sept. 10, a clear head-and-shoulders pattern has formed in the 10-year yield so what I said above can break that lower and get us sub-7% rates. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they’re still trending near multi-year lows. I can’t stress enough how important it is for spreads to be closer to 2% than 3%, since mortgage rates would already be over 8% now if this were not the case. Not only that, it would have been impossible to get mortgage rates near 7% again without a much bigger move lower with the 10-year yield. That said, when the 10-year yield moves lower at times, spreads can widen after a big move up because their job is to compress volatility. Now, this does wear off over time, and we can head lower again. What you don’t want to see is the Fed suddenly changing course and starting a massive rate-hike cycle, or a credit event like the Silicon Valley Bank crisis. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads were flat at 2.23% from week to week. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been over the last three years, given the 10-year yield’s current level: If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.15% today, not 7.27%. If we had the worst levels of 2024, mortgage rates would be 7.77% today. If we had the worst levels of 2025, mortgage rates would be 7.58% today. Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. The key for the last two weeks: lower rates even above 7%, have stabilized demand, as our weekly pending home sales are still higher than two weeks ago. That is all we should take from this move, and we will see how rates affect the data going forward. Rule of thumb for the last three years and 10 months: housing demand typically grows when rates are under 6.64% and heading toward 6%, and doesn’t show growth when rates are over 6.64% and heading above 7%. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 52,050 2025: 55,214 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. I expected some week-to-week growth last week, as our tracker showed growth too; we did have a 4% week-to-week gain, but it's still down significantly year over year. When rates were closer to 6%, every week except one showed year-over-year growth. Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026: 16 positive week-to-week prints 23 negative week-to-week prints 5 flat week-to-week prints 10 weeks of double-digit year-over-year growth 25 weeks of positive year-over-year growth 14 negative year-over-year prints Housing inventory Housing inventory growth has been very tame this year, with some weeks down year-over-year. In fact, this is the lowest inventory growth in some time. Mostly because rates were lower at the start of the year and we are closer to normal. However, higher mortgage rates and weaker mortgage demand create more inventory, and the year-over-year comps are much easier now than early in the year. These lower comps will be here until July of 2027. Inventory growth is running at 6.78% even with easier comps. Rent trends have been mixed in recent periods. While rents declined in several submarkets, the largest decreases occurred in Santa Ana and Anaheim, which had recently been among the strongest areas for rent growth. The recent decline appears to be more of a correction following outsized gains than evidence of a broader pullback in achievable rents.Multifamily investment activity has increased this year, with the market on pace to record its highest transaction count since 2022. Track apartment market trends in our latest MarketBeat report, including supply, demand, and pricing. DOWNLOAD Q3 2026 REPORT Key MULTIFAMILY Takeaways For Q3 2026 Vacancy fell to its lowest level in three years. The national vacancy rate dropped 30 basis points (bps) quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) to 8.6%, the third consecutive quarterly decline. Vacancy is now more than 90 bps below its Q4 2025 peak. Demand continues to outrun new supply. Year-to-date (YTD) net absorption totaled nearly 350,000 units, up 14% year-over-year (YOY), the strongest first three quarters since 2021. Meanwhile, YTD deliveries fell 25% YOY to just over 250,000 units. Rent growth reached its fastest pace since early 2023. Asking rents rose 2.3% YOY to $1,950, more than double the 1.1% trough in the first quarter. For the data behind the commentary, download the full Q3 2026 U.S. Multifamily Report. Demand Is Running at Its Strongest Pace Since 2021 National vacancy fell 30 bps QOQ to 8.6% in Q3, hitting the lowest reading since Q3 2023 after three consecutive quarterly declines. Although vacancy remains roughly 140 bps above the long-run trend, the sustained improvement points to a multifamily market firmly in recovery. Strong demand is the clear driver. YTD absorption reached nearly 350,000 units, 14% above the same period last year and the strongest first three quarters of any year except 2021. A resilient economy continues to support household formation and renter demand, while higher interest rates and elevated home prices have widened the affordability gap between renting and owning. Texas continues to lead the demand recovery, with three of its markets among the nation's top five for absorption. Dallas/Ft. Worth leads with more than 50,000 units this year, followed by New York (37,000), Austin (34,000), Phoenix (31,000) and Houston (26,000 units). On a percentage basis, Sarasota (6.7% of inventory), Savannah (5.3%) and Boise (5.1%) saw the largest YTD increases. Supply-heavy markets such as Charlotte (4.4%) and Denver (3.7%) also rank in the top 20 as new lease-ups fill. New Supply Keeps Shrinking Deliveries totaled roughly 250,000 units through the first three quarters of 2026, down 25% from 335,000 units in the same period of 2025 and the lowest YTD total since 2021. The supply pipeline is set to slow further, with fewer than 480,000 units underway, the lowest level on a nominal basis since 2015. As a share of existing inventory, the construction pipeline stands at just 3.6%, the lowest since 2013 and less than half its recent peak. The pullback in construction activity is broad-based. More than 70% of the 90 markets tracked by Cushman & Wakefield Research have smaller construction pipelines than a year ago. The steepest declines came in the markets that built most aggressively during the boom. Sarasota's pipeline fell 790 bps as a share of inventory, while Savannah (-240 bps), Austin (-220 bps), Phoenix (-200 bps) and Salt Lake City (-200 bps) also recorded significant declines. Several Midwest markets pulled back sharply as well, led by Columbus (-330 bps) and Madison (-310 bps). Pipelines expanded in just 25 markets, most notably Palm Beach and the Bay Area, where stronger rent growth has improved developer economics. Rent Growth Accelerates as Occupancy Improves National asking rents rose 2.3% YOY to $1,950 in Q3, the fastest annual pace since Q1 2023 but roughly half the pre-pandemic average. Annual growth has more than doubled from its 1.1% trough in Q1 2026 as demand strengthened, and absorption outpaced deliveries in every quarter this year. Favorable base effects also contributed, as rents softened in the second half of 2025. The rent recovery is spreading beyond the Northeast and Midwest, which have led the nation since 2023. The West has seen the sharpest turnaround, with rent growth climbing from 0.6% at the end of 2025 to 2.6% in Q3, its strongest pace since late 2022. The Bay Area is driving much of that gain. San Francisco leads the nation at nearly 16% YOY growth, followed by San Jose (9%) and the East Bay (6.9%), as AI-related investment and job growth support renewed renter demand and greater landlord pricing power. Outside the Bay Area, rent growth across the West averaged a more modest 1.9%. items.title: Hidden Costs of Homeownership Top $16.6K a Year as Insurance Climbs
items.description: Hidden Costs of Homeownership Top $16.6K a Year as Insurance Climbs The typical U.S. homeowner pays $16,566 a year, about $1,380 a month, for maintenance, property taxes and insurance on top of a mortgage payment. Written by Kara Ng on October 22, 2026 The typical U.S. homeowner pays $16,566 a year, about $1,380 a month, for maintenance, property taxes and insurance on top of a mortgage payment, a new Zillow and Thumbtack analysis finds. That total is up 3% in the past year. Insurance premiums are up 54% in five years, outpacing maintenance (32%) and property taxes (19%). In Houston, Phoenix, Denver and Nashville, homeowners now pay more for insurance than for property taxes. Hidden costs range from $14,187 a year in Phoenix to $25,111 in New York. Maintenance is the largest cost in every metro analyzed. Many households focus on winning the home and underestimate what it costs to live in it, and those recurring costs add to the affordability challenge of homeownership. Here is how the hidden costs break down for the typical U.S. homeowner: Maintenance: $11,171 a year, about two-thirds of the total Property taxes: $3,129 a year (estimated) Homeowners insurance: $2,266 a year (estimated) Insurance is the fastest-rising cost Over the past five years, insurance premiums have risen 54%, compared with 32% for maintenance and 19% for property taxes. That shift is changing the math in some of the country's biggest metro areas. In Houston, Phoenix, Denver and Nashville, the typical homeowner now pays more each year for insurance than for property taxes. Premiums are up at least 50% over five years in 19 of the 30 metros analyzed. The steepest increases are in Dallas (75%), Tampa (71%), Denver (70%) and Houston (69%). Miami homeowners pay the most for insurance at nearly $5,000 a year, up 62% in five years. Six metros now top $3,000 a year: Miami, Dallas, Houston, Tampa, Orlando and Denver. Maintenance remains the largest cost Maintenance is the largest hidden cost in every metro analyzed, and it tops $12K in Seattle ($12,594) and Boston ($12,486). Los Angeles saw the sharpest year-over-year jump in maintenance costs, at 27%. The increase was primarily driven by ongoing wildfire recovery efforts, heightened demand for residential services and elevated labor costs. Hidden costs are highest in expensive coastal metros Total hidden costs are highest in New York ($25,111), San Francisco ($24,383), Boston ($22,096), and Seattle ($21,354). Even in Phoenix, the least costly metro analyzed, they run $14,187 a year. Over five years, hidden costs rose the most in Pittsburgh (54.8%), Tampa (44.4%), Miami (42.8%) and Los Angeles (42.5%). New York, where costs are already highest, rose the least, at 13.8%. Methodology Zillow estimated annual property tax and homeowners insurance costs for a typical U.S. homeowner in each of 30 metros, then compared year-over-year and five-year changes. Thumbtack provided estimates for annual home maintenance costs, based on projects requested on Thumbtack and reported directly by the independent service professional or individual customer. The maintenance cost is an unweighted index of yearly home maintenance projects, calculated quarterly using a moving average. items.title: National Home Value Growth Accelerates Yet Continues To Trail Inflation
items.description: Trends Follow Us On Google National Home Value Growth Accelerates Yet Continues To Trail Inflation By Snejana Farberov October 27, 2026 SeanPavonePhoto/Adobe Stock National home values posted modest gains in August, picking up speed from July, though price growth still failed to keep pace with inflation. The value of single-family homes as measured by repeat transactions rose 2.1% year over year in August, up from a 1.9% annual increase the month before, according to data from the S P Cotality Case-Shiller Index released Tuesday. The more robust growth came even as the median existing-home sales price slowed to a 1.6% annual gain in August. However, while nominal home values accelerated nationally, they fell in real terms for the 15th consecutive month, as August's 3.4% inflation rate ran roughly 1.3 percentage points above the home value gain. Across the 20 cities tracked by the index, Chicago once again took pole position, leading the U.S. for the sixth consecutive month with a 6.7% annual gain, down slightly from July. New York followed with a year-over-year increase of 6.2%. Cleveland took bronze, registering a gain of 4.3%. "Seasonality continued to weigh on headline monthly results," says Rebecca Kaufman , associate director of commodities at S P Dow Jones Indices. "On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, the U.S. National and 10-City Composite Indices fell 0.2% and 0.4%, respectively, while their seasonally adjusted counterparts rose 0.3% and 0.4%. The divergence suggests that the typical post-summer slowdown is obscuring some underlying strength in home prices." Loading... However, Kaufman concedes that affordability remains a challenge. Referring to August data before mortgage rates crossed the 7% threshold, she notes: "With inflation at 3.4%, Brent crude near $100 per barrel and mortgage rates in the mid-to-high 6% range, households continue to face elevated costs alongside persistently high home prices." The latest Case-Shiller report highlights a persistent regional divergence in home prices. Seattle posted the nation's steepest annual decline for the third month in a row, slipping 1.6%, followed by Las Vegas (-1.3%), and Denver (-0.8%). "The years-long East-West divide persists, with six out of the eight Eastern metropolitan markets recording greater year-over-year changes in July versus June, compared with just two of the eight Western metropolitan markets," says Kaufman. As in June and July, a gap of nearly 9 percentage points separated the strongest housing market, Chicago, which was bolstered by tight resale supply and limited new construction, from the weakest, Seattle. Loading... What this means for homebuyers Looking ahead, Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith reminds that the rate backdrop has become considerably more challenging since the end of August. The 30-year fixed rate climbed to 7.40% in mid-October, the highest level of the year, before easing to 7.32% as of Oct. 22 , after the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate on Sept. 16 and September Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose to 3.7%. Pending home sales plunged 7.3% in September to the lowest reading on record and were down 11.3% from a year ago, with declines in all four regions. "With inventory at its highest level since 2019 and rates above 7%, buyers have more homes to choose from but less power to pay for them," says Smith. The Case-Shiller Index reports on a two-month delay and reflects a three-month moving average of home sales prices. Homes usually go under contract a month or two before they close, so the August report primarily reflects purchase decisions made in late spring and early summer. Although the Index's price data is delayed by several months, it is considered one of the best available measures of changing home values, because it is based on repeat transactions on the same properties. items.title: Slightly lower mortgage rates finally pause slide in housing demand
items.description: Lower mortgage rates finally stopped the decline in housing demand last week. After mortgage rates peaked around 7.60% and fell toward 7.30%, housing demand stopped bleeding temporarily, and we saw a smidge of growth during one of the bond market's more volatile weeks in 2026. As we enter the last week of October, let’s review what happened with the 10-year yield, mortgage rates and housing demand and what it means for the rest of year. 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% What a crazy week in the bond market! On Friday’s podcast , Editor and Chief Sarah Wheeler and I discussed the madness of what happened, but to be honest, the whole month has been based on the 10-year yield holding the 5.35% level. Even with elevated oil prices and firm economic data, that key level holding and some weakness in the AI story brought the 10-year yield back below 5% last week, so mortgage rates are slightly lower than their peak. For now, the worst-case scenario of 8% and even 9% mortgage rates that people have been talking about is off the table—as long as we hold that 5.35% level, we can get this conflict over with and oil prices fall again. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened since the year's lows, but they're still trending near cycle lows since the Fed started its rate-hike cycle in 2022. I can’t stress enough how important it is for spreads to be closer to 2% than 3%. That said, when the 10-year yield moves sharply lower, spreads do tend to widen, since they're designed to limit volatility, so their recent move higher makes sense. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.23%, up from 2.21% the week before. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been over the last three years, given the 10-year yield’s current level: If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.21% today, not 7.33%. If we had the worst levels of 2024, mortgage rates would be 7.83% today. If we had the worst levels of 2025, mortgage rates would be 7.64% today. Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. This week, the bleeding stopped. As mortgage rates fell slightly, the week-to-week data finally stopped declining, and we saw a slight positive print. But I wouldn’t make too much of the improvement this week, as the weekly data was softening faster, and it doesn’t take much to stop the bleeding. Housing demand typically grows like it did for the first half of 2026 when mortgage rates are under 6.64%. In fact, the only thing that slowed demand in the first part of the year was the holiday and snowstorm. However, rates above 7% have always created softer data in the last 3 years and 10 months. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 52,490 2025: 67,752 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. This week’s print obviously doesn’t account for the rate move over the last few days, so we'll see if we get week-to-week growth next week. However, you can see the damage done here with rates above 7%, as purchase applications are once again down week-to-week and year over year. Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026: 15 positive week-to-week prints 23 negative week-to-week prints 5 flat week-to-week prints 10 weeks of double-digit year-over-year growth 25 weeks of positive year-over-year growth 13 negative year-over-year prints Housing inventory Housing inventory growth has been very tame this year, with some weeks down year-over-year. However, as always, when rates rise, especially above 7%, inventory can grow faster. Inventory growth has been slower than in previous years, mostly because we are closer to normal inventory levels. With that said, inventory growth has picked up since mid-August, and the year-over-year comps are much easier to show growth, as mortgage rates were 1% lower last year and demand was heading toward a 9-month high in December 2025. Inventory growth is running at 5.68% even with easier comps. Weekly inventory change (Oct. 16-Oct. 23): Inventory rose from 905,166 to 911,956 Same week last year (Oct. 19-Oct. 24): Inventory rose from 859,424 to 862,924 New listings New listings are in their typical seasonal decline; 2026 has been the healthiest new-listings year since 2022, with over 80,000 at a few points this year. One concern I have with rates at current levels is that some sellers might not list because most sellers are also homebuyers. We saw a year-over-year decline this week — this is something I will keep an eye out for the rest of the year to see if this becomes a trend, but so far 2026 has been the best year for new listings in a while. In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years . Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years: 2026: 60,151 2025: 64,191 Price-cut percentage Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This was true until rates moved above 6.64% and, once above 7%, with demand falling, the price-cut percentage is 1% higher year over year.
