items.title: Fundamentals Take the Lead as Capital Stays Selective
items.description: Fundamentals Take the Lead as Capital Stays Selective Oct 21, 2026 | 5 min read U.S. Capital Markets Snapshot Report | Q3 2026 Property fundamentals continued to improve during the third quarter even as capital remained selective. Download Report Experts David Amsterdam President, Capital Markets | U.S. David Goodhue Executive Managing Director | Boston & Head of Multifamily Capital Markets | U.S Rachael Rothman Director, National Capital Markets Research Share Article Key Themes Improving property fundamentals are increasingly driving investment decisions. Capital remains selective, favoring assets with durable cash flow and limited competition. Distress continues to create opportunities, particularly within the office sector. Slowing development activity is supporting long-term occupancy and rent growth across several sectors. Multifamily: Recovery Becomes Increasingly Regional Multifamily is entering a more favorable phase as construction pipelines continue to contract and supply pressures ease. However, performance is becoming increasingly market-specific, with West Coast asking rents rising 3.2% year over year while several East Coast and Sun Belt markets continue to work through elevated supply levels. Office: Distress Creates Opportunity Office investment activity continues to gain traction in select markets as improving leasing conditions and deeply reset values attract capital. Demand remains concentrated in trophy and well-located properties, while elevated distress and refinancing pressure continue to create recapitalization, restructuring, and acquisition opportunities across the sector. Industrial: Liquidity Remains Strong Industrial remains one of the most liquid and institutionally favored asset classes. Sales volume reached its highest Q1-Q3 level since 2022, while durable occupier demand and a slowing development pipeline continue to support investor interest. Retail: Supply-Demand Fundamentals Remain Strong Retail continues to benefit from limited new supply, healthy occupancy, and steady consumer demand. Grocery-anchored and necessity-based formats remain highly sought after, supported by durable cash flows and a retail environment increasingly shaped by omnichannel shopping strategies. Hospitality: Operating Fundamentals Continue to Improve Hospitality investment activity is strengthening as limited new construction supports operating performance. RevPAR growth rebounded in September as demand strengthened across the market, supported by group travel and continued domestic demand. Questions This Report Answers Q: What are the current cap rates for core commercial real estate sectors? A: As of Q3 2026, core cap rates are 5.4% for multifamily, 7.4% for office, 5.1% for industrial, 6.6% for malls and 6.3% for strip centers within the retail sector, and 8.5% for hospitality, reflecting continued variation in pricing and investor sentiment across major property sectors. Q: How is the multifamily recovery evolving across U.S. markets? A: The development pipeline continues to shrink, reducing future supply pressures. At the same time, performance is diverging by region, with West Coast markets outperforming many East Coast and Sun Belt markets. Q: What is driving investment activity in the office sector despite elevated distress? A: Improving leasing activity, limited new supply, and deeply reset property values are creating opportunities for buyers focused on high-quality assets and value-add repositioning strategies. Q: Why does industrial remain a preferred allocation for institutional capital? A: Durable tenant demand, sustained transaction volume, slowing supply growth, and confidence in long-term demand drivers continue to make industrial one of the most attractive sectors for institutional investors. Q: How are investors approaching the retail sector in an omnichannel environment? A: Investors remain focused on grocery-anchored and necessity-based formats that complement evolving consumer shopping behaviors while providing stable cash flow and limited competitive supply. items.title: Bank of America pegs 2027 mortgage volume at $1.72T, warns of 2023-style housing replay
items.description: Bank of America projects muted mortgage growth in 2027, with total originations reaching $1.719 trillion and only about $344 billion coming from refinances, according to a report released Friday. The bank’s analysts said their outlook is “slightly lower” than other industry forecasts because they expect weaker housing market conditions and home sales, along with “a marginally higher projected year-end rate level.” Their 2027 forecast is the third major call for origination volume to remain below $2 trillion next year. The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) expects total single-family originations to fall 5% to $1.99 trillion in 2027. Fannie Mae is forecasting $1.86 trillion for next year. BofA’s forecast represents a decline of 15% compared to the $2.030 trillion expected for 2026. It assumes a 10-year Treasury yield average of 5.25% in 2027, a 2.5% year-over-year decline in existing home sales , an 0.5% increase in new home sales and a 1% rise in full-year home price appreciation. Secondary market On the capital markets side, BofA analysts expect agency mortgage-backed securities gross issuance of a little more than $1.12 trillion in 2027, down from about $1.33 trillion this year. Weaker issuance is being driven by softer home sales, a higher share of all-cash transactions in a high-rate environment, a smaller contribution from warehouse pipeline effects, and more agency collateral flowing into nonagency securitizations . These headwinds are only partially offset by modest gains in cash-out refis and lower portfolio retention by the government-sponsored enterprises, the analysts said. Replay of 2023? BofA frames 2027 as a replay of 2023 in several key respects: elevated mortgage rates , subdued housing activity, affordability challenges and a persistent lock-in effect. But the analysts argue that 2027 could be “even more challenging” than 2023 because several demand-supportive forces have faded. In 2023, many buyers still believed higher mortgage rates were temporary and leaned on a “buy now, refinance later” strategy. By 2027, rates will have been elevated for nearly five years, and the Federal Reserve will have resumed tightening , eroding confidence in meaningful refinance opportunities. At the same time, home price appreciation has cooled while homeownership looks more like a high-carry, lower-return investment. In addition, the reversal of the work-from-home trend has removed a major tailwind that boosted housing demand during and after the pandemic. The bank does see some offsets. The lock-in effect has eased modestly at the market level as more higher-rate loans have been originated in recent years, slightly increasing the pool of borrowers who could benefit from future rate relief. Housing supply conditions have improved compared to the tightest pandemic-era levels, and some large markets, including parts of Florida , are showing localized signs of recovery. items.title: Single-Family Development Remains Constrained
items.description: Single-Family Development Remains Constrained by Chuck Ehmann Posted October 21, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits Don't expect single-family construction to accelerate anytime soon. Consumer and builder confidence has weakened, while mortgage rates, financing costs, construction expenses, labor costs and regulatory hurdles continue to weigh on development activity. At the same time, ongoing affordability concerns and elevated home prices are limiting housing demand. Single-family housing starts surged above 1.3 million units on a seasonally adjusted basis during the post-pandemic period of exceptionally low mortgage rates. As borrowing costs climbed and mortgage rates moved above 7%, housing starts fell to roughly 800,000 units by late 2022. Annualized starts activity later recovered to more than one million units before gradually easing back toward 900,000 units in 2026. With mortgage rates averaging roughly 7.4% in October, pressure on the single-family sector is likely to persist. September’s seasonally adjusted rate for single-family starts was 859,000 units, down 4.6% from August’s revised rate but up 2.6% from one year ago. Annualized single-family permits fell 4% from August and 4.8% from last September to a 3.5-year low of 845,000 units. The number of single-family homes currently under construction was unchanged month-to-month at 587,000 units, but that annualized rate was down 2.8% from last September. Single-family completions dipped 2.4% for the month but fell 11% from one year ago to 840,000 units, while units authorized, but not started jumped 6.3% from last year to 151,000 units, the same rate as last month. Meanwhile, multifamily development faces similar headwinds with the seasonally adjusted starts rate at 349,000 units, down 7.2% from August and 25.9% from last year. Annualized multifamily permitting increased 5.9% for the month and 1% for the year to 503,000 units. Reflecting the volatility of the seasonally adjusted data series, the unadjusted annual starts and permits totals for multifamily were both up close to 7% from last September. Like the single-family series, the annualized rate of multifamily units under construction was unchanged for the month at 677,000 units, however, that was down 3.1% for the year. Authorized multifamily units that were not started were also unchanged for the month at 123,000 units but were up 13.9% for the year. Multifamily completions rose 14.9% from August to 339,000 units but were down 20.4% for the year. Compared to one year ago, the annual rate for multifamily permitting increased in two of the four regions, with moderate improvement in the Northeast (up 8.5% to 83,000 units) and solid growth in the Midwest (up 32.8% to 79,000 units). The West region saw the deepest decrease of 17% in annual multifamily permitting to 100,000 units in September, followed by a very modest 0.2% decrease in the South to 241,000 units. Compared to the previous month, permitting was down in the West and up in the remaining regions. Annualized multifamily starts decreased sharply in three regions: the West (down 56.7% to 48,000 units), the Midwest (down 54.4% to 35,000 units) and the Northeast (down 43.5% to 62,000 units). The South region’s multifamily starts increased 16.8% to 205,000 units. Compared to August’s seasonally adjusted annual rate, starts were up strongly in the South and down in the remaining regions. items.title: The housing market gets a positive Fed day for a change
items.description: On Wednesday we got an October surprise: the Fed day was eerily calm, with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh looking comfortable on stage and offering a slightly dovish take on the future — if a few things improve. I believe the Fed wants to take back all the interest rate cuts from last year, and then they can assess what is happening in the economy. Of course, the Iran conflict and Trade War 2.0 have complicated their job, but today, given that markets were at one point pricing in five to six rate hikes, was a positive day. Last I checked, the 10-year was at 5.02%, down after Google reported a bad quarter. The Fed's press statement was short and simple, but two things caught my attention. 1. The economy is strong vs. solid First, the Fed chose to use the word "strong" instead of "solid" on purpose to signal it won’t cut rates and will continue reversing last year's interest rate cuts while inflation stays above target. “ Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.” Warsh said jobless claims data remain low and that the Fed fully intends to bring inflation back to the 2% target, no compromise. He also said the Fed will hold one fewer voting meeting in 2027 and two fewer meetings in 2028; this approach might leave the Fed open to more 50-basis-point cuts or hikes. However, that is another story for another time. 2. Warsh liked the market drama against AI I got a strong sense that Warsh liked the market getting more restrictive and that we even saw some AI companies shed some blood recently. My theme in the HousingWire Daily podcast lately borrows from The Predator movie: the AI god king can bleed — and that it means you can kill it. I think Warsh was implying no company is invincible, and that if the market gets more restrictive, things can change, as they recently did. He also talked about how the 10-year yield rolled over even though oil prices have been elevated this month. I believe the 10-year yield rollover is more market-driven, as the 10-year was pricing in more rate hikes than the Fed was targeting at the time. The term premium on the 10-year yield was elevated as it headed to the October high. If the 10-year had closed over the key level of 5.35%, bond yields had the potential to rise much higher, faster, as the markets would be pricing in a much more aggressive Fed rate hike cycle, but, smartly, they chose not to go that route. Warsh seems to enjoy that everyone is taking the Fed seriously and that the markets have already done a lot of the work for them. This reaffirms my assumption that all they want to do is take back the rate cuts from last year and then reassess what is going on. One side note was that Fed Governor Lisa Cook — who is usually a dove — voted to raise rates, which I 100% believe was a trolling tactic on her part since Trump still wants to fire her . All in all, it wasn’t a bad day; the 10-year yield is above 5% still today, but considering the market was trying to price in five to six rate hikes, and there hasn’t been any end to the conflict or the trade war, I consider this a victory for the month of October. For housing, the worst-case scenario has been averted and we bought some time, giving space for the conflict to end and the trade war to cool off a bit. What I am hoping for is that we get some more clarity on both of those two items, and then the Fed can make the rate hike cycle just a few rate hikes, and then we'll take it from there.
